title: Part 2, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Which relates the strange thing, one that might well be called an adventure, that befell Don Quixote

A clear, fresh spring they came upon in a cool grove washed away the dust and weariness that the bulls’ rude treatment had left on Don Quixote and Sancho, and beside it, after turning Dapple and Rocinante loose without halter or bridle, the dejected pair, master and servant, sat down. Sancho went to the storehouse of his saddlebags and brought out of them what he liked to call the grub; Don Quixote rinsed his mouth and bathed his face, and the cool water revived his drooping spirits. Out of sheer vexation he ate nothing, and out of sheer courtesy Sancho did not dare touch a bite of what lay before him, but waited for his master to taste it first. Seeing, though, that Don Quixote, lost in his thoughts, was forgetting to lift the bread to his lips, he said not a word, and, trampling every rule of good manners underfoot, began packing into his belly whatever bread and cheese came to hand.

“Eat, Sancho my friend,” said Don Quixote; “sustain your life, which matters more to you than mine does to me, and leave me to die under the weight of my thoughts and the press of my misfortunes. I was born, Sancho, to live dying, and you to die eating; and to see how true this is, consider me: printed in histories, famous in arms, courteous in conduct, honored by princes, courted by maidens — and yet, just when I was looking forward to the palms, triumphs, and crowns that my valiant deeds had won and earned, I found myself this very morning trodden down, kicked, and pounded under the hooves of filthy, unclean beasts. The thought of it dulls my teeth, numbs my jaws, cripples my hands, and strips me of all appetite for food — so much so that I have half a mind to let myself die of hunger, the cruelest of all deaths.”

“So then,” said Sancho, chewing busily all the while, “your worship doesn’t hold with the proverb that says, ‘Let Martha die, so long as she dies with a full belly.’ I, at any rate, have no intention of killing myself; far from it — I mean to do what the cobbler does, who stretches the leather with his teeth until it reaches as far as he needs. I’ll stretch my life out by eating until it reaches the end heaven has set for it; and let me tell you, señor, there’s no greater madness than wanting to die of despair, the way your worship does. Take my advice: after you’ve eaten, lie down and sleep a while on this green mattress of grass, and you’ll find that when you wake you’ll feel a good deal better.”

Don Quixote did as he suggested, for Sancho’s reasoning struck him as more a philosopher’s than a fool’s, and he said, “Sancho, if you would do for me what I am about to ask, my relief would be more certain and my heaviness of heart not so great. It is this: while I sleep, following your advice, go off a little way, bare your flesh to the open air, and give yourself three or four hundred lashes with Rocinante’s reins, on account of the three thousand and some you are bound to give yourself for Dulcinea’s disenchantment; for it is a great pity that the poor lady should remain enchanted through your carelessness and neglect.”

“There’s a good deal to be said about that,” said Sancho; “for now let’s both get some sleep, and after that, God has already decreed what will happen. Your worship should know that whipping oneself in cold blood is a hard business, especially when the lashes land on a body that’s badly nourished and worse fed. Let my lady Dulcinea be patient; when she’s least expecting it she’ll see me whipped till I look like a sieve, and ‘until death it’s all life’ — I mean, I still have life in me, along with the will to make good what I’ve promised.”

Don Quixote thanked him, ate a little, and Sancho ate a great deal, and then the two of them lay down to sleep, leaving those inseparable friends and companions, Rocinante and Dapple, to their own devices, free to graze at will on the plentiful grass the meadow offered. They woke fairly late, mounted again, and continued on their way, pressing forward to reach an inn that appeared to be about a league off. I say an inn, because Don Quixote called it one, against his usual habit of calling every inn a castle. When they arrived, they asked the landlord whether they could lodge there. He said yes, and with all the comfort and good fare they could find in Saragossa. They dismounted, and Sancho stowed his provisions in a room to which the landlord gave him the key. He led the animals to the stable, gave them their feed, and came back to see what orders Don Quixote — who was seated on a bench by the door — might have for him, offering particular thanks to heaven that his master had not taken this inn for a castle. Supper-time came; they withdrew to their room, and Sancho asked the landlord what he had to give them for supper. The landlord replied that his mouth should be the measure: he had only to ask for whatever he liked, since that inn was stocked with the birds of the air, the fowls of the earth, and the fish of the sea.
“No need for all that,” said Sancho; “if they’ll roast us a couple of chickens we’ll be content, for my master is delicate and eats little, and I’m not excessively greedy myself.”
The landlord answered that he had no chickens, because the kites had carried them off.
“In that case,” said Sancho, “let señor landlord have a pullet roasted, and see that it’s a tender one.”
“A pullet! By my father!” said the landlord; “the honest truth is that only yesterday I sent more than fifty off to the city to sell. But apart from pullets, ask for anything you please.”
“Then surely,” said Sancho, “you won’t be short of veal or kid.”
“Just at the moment,” said the landlord, “there’s none in the house, because it’s all run out; but next week there will be more than enough.”
“A lot of good that does us,” said Sancho; “I’d lay a bet that all these shortages are going to end up amounting to plenty of bacon and eggs.”

“By God,” said the landlord, “my guest must be slow-witted indeed; I tell him I have neither pullets nor hens, and he wants me to have eggs! Run through some other delicacies, if you please, and stop asking about anything in the way of poultry.”
“Body of me!” said Sancho, “let’s settle this: tell me once and for all what you do have, and let’s waste no more words on it.”

“What I truly and honestly have, señor guest,” said the landlord, “is a pair of cow-heels that look like calves’ feet, or a pair of calves’ feet that look like cow-heels; they’re stewed with chickpeas, onions, and bacon, and at this very moment they’re calling out, ‘Come and eat me, come and eat me.’”

“I claim them as mine here and now,” said Sancho; “let no one lay a hand on them. I’ll pay better for them than anyone else would, because nothing could suit my taste more, and it doesn’t matter a pin to me whether they’re feet or heels.”
“No one shall touch them,” said the landlord; “for the other guests I have, being people of high rank, travel with their own cook, caterer, and larder.”

“If it’s a question of rank,” said Sancho, “nobody outranks my master; but the calling he follows allows for no larders or pantries. We simply stretch ourselves out in the middle of a meadow and fill up on acorns or medlars.”

There the conversation between Sancho and the landlord ended, Sancho having no wish to carry it further by answering him; for the landlord had already asked him what calling or what profession it was his master followed.

When supper-time came, then, Don Quixote retired to his room, the landlord brought in the stew-pot just as it was, and he sat down to eat with great determination. It seems that in another room, next to Don Quixote’s and separated from it by nothing more than a thin partition, he overheard these words: “On your life, Señor Don Jeronimo, while supper is being brought, let us read another chapter of the Second Part of ‘Don Quixote of La Mancha.’”

The instant Don Quixote heard his own name he sprang to his feet and listened with sharpened ears to catch what they were saying about him, and he heard the Don Jeronimo who had been addressed reply, “Why would you have us read such nonsense, Don Juan, when no one who has read the First Part of the history of ‘Don Quixote of La Mancha’ can possibly take any pleasure in reading this Second Part?”

“Even so,” said the one called Don Juan, “we would do well to read it, since there is no book so bad that it doesn’t contain something good. What displeases me most about this one is that it portrays Don Quixote as cured by now of his love for Dulcinea del Toboso.”

At this Don Quixote, full of rage and indignation, raised his voice and said, “Whoever says that Don Quixote of La Mancha has forgotten, or could ever forget, Dulcinea del Toboso, I will teach him with equal arms how far he stands from the truth; for the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso cannot be forgotten, nor can forgetfulness find any room in Don Quixote. Constancy is his motto, and his profession is to uphold it with his life and never betray it.”
“Who is it that answers us?” said those in the next room.
“Who should it be,” said Sancho, “but Don Quixote of La Mancha himself, who will stand behind everything he has said and everything he has yet to say? A good payer isn’t troubled by his pledges.”

Sancho had hardly spoken these words when two gentlemen — for such they appeared to be — came into the room, and one of them, throwing his arms around Don Quixote’s neck, said to him, “Your appearance leaves no doubt about your name, nor can your name fail to vouch for your appearance: beyond question, señor, you are the true Don Quixote of La Mancha, north star and morning light of knight-errantry, in spite and in defiance of the man who has tried to usurp your name and wipe out your achievements, as the author of this book I here present to you has done.” With that he placed a book his companion was carrying into Don Quixote’s hands; Don Quixote took it and, without a word, began running his eye over it, but shortly handed it back, saying, “In the little I have seen, I have found three things in this author that deserve censure. The first is certain words I have read in the preface; the second, that the language is Aragonese, since he sometimes writes without articles; and the third — the one that above all convicts him of ignorance — is that he blunders and strays from the truth in the most essential point of the history, for here he says that the wife of my squire Sancho Panza is named Mari Gutierrez, when she is called no such thing, but Teresa Panza; and when a man gets so important a point wrong, there is good reason to fear he is wrong about every other point in the history.”

“A fine sort of historian, to be sure!” cried Sancho at this; “he must know a great deal about our affairs, if he calls my wife Teresa Panza Mari Gutierrez. Take the book back, señor, and see whether I’m in it and whether he’s changed my name too.”
“From the way you talk, friend,” said Don Jeronimo, “you must surely be Sancho Panza, Señor Don Quixote’s squire.”
“I am,” said Sancho; “and proud of it.”

“Well then, by my faith,” said the gentleman, “this new author doesn’t treat you with the decency your person displays. He makes you out a gross feeder and a simpleton, not in the least amusing — a very different creature from the Sancho described in the First Part of your master’s history.”
“God forgive him,” said Sancho; “he could have left me in my corner without troubling his head about me at all. ‘Let him who knows how, ring the bells’; ‘Saint Peter is well off in Rome.’”

The two gentlemen urged Don Quixote to come to their room and share their supper, for they knew very well there was nothing in that inn fit for a man of his quality. Don Quixote, courteous as ever, yielded to their invitation and supped with them. Sancho stayed behind with the stew, and, vested with full delegated authority, seated himself at the head of the table, with the landlord beside him, who was every bit as devoted to cow-heels and calves’ feet as Sancho was.

Over supper Don Juan asked Don Quixote what news he had of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso: was she married, had she given birth, was she with child, or did she remain a maiden — keeping her modesty and delicacy intact — and still cherish the memory of Señor Don Quixote’s tender devotion?

To this he replied, “Dulcinea is a maiden still, my passion more deeply rooted than ever, our dealings as unrewarding as before, and her beauty transformed into that of a coarse peasant girl.” Then he went on to give them a full and detailed account of Dulcinea’s enchantment, of what had befallen him in the cave of Montesinos, and of the remedy the sage Merlin had prescribed for her disenchantment — namely, the whipping of Sancho.

The two gentlemen took the greatest delight in hearing Don Quixote relate the strange events of his history, and they were as much astonished by his absurdities as by the elegant style in which he delivered them. At one moment they took him for a man of intelligence and good sense; at the next he seemed to them a rambling fool; and they could not settle where, between wisdom and folly, they ought to place him.

Sancho, having finished his supper and left the landlord laid out in the shape of an X, went off to the room where his master was, and as he came in he said, “Strike me dead, sirs, if the author of that book your worships have there wants the two of us to stay on good terms. Since he calls me a glutton — according to what your worships say — I only hope he doesn’t call me a drunkard as well.”

“He does call you that,” said Don Jeronimo; “though I can’t recall just how he puts it. I know only that his words are offensive, and lies besides, as I can see plainly enough from the face of the worthy Sancho here before me.”

“Take my word for it,” said Sancho, “the Sancho and the Don Quixote in that history must be different people from the ones who appear in the history Cide Hamete Benengeli wrote — which is to say, ourselves: my master valiant, wise, and true in love; and I simple and droll, and neither a glutton nor a drunkard.”

“I believe it,” said Don Juan; “and if it were possible, an order ought to be issued that no one presume to deal with anything concerning Don Quixote except Cide Hamete, his original author — just as Alexander commanded that no one presume to paint his portrait but Apelles.”
“Let anyone who pleases paint me,” said Don Quixote, “but let him not mistreat me; for patience will often give way when insults are heaped upon it.”

“No insult can be offered to Señor Don Quixote,” said Don Juan, “that he is not able to avenge — unless he turns it aside with the shield of his patience, which, by my reckoning, is great and strong.”

A good part of the night went by in talk of this kind, and though Don Juan wanted Don Quixote to read more of the book and see how it went on, he could not be persuaded. He said that he considered it read, pronounced the whole of it foolish, and added that if it should somehow reach the author’s ears that he had held it in his hands, he did not want the man flattering himself that Don Quixote had actually read it; for our thoughts — and our eyes still more — should keep their distance from whatever is obscene and foul.

They asked him where he intended to go next. He answered, to Saragossa, to take part in the jousts in armor that were held in that city every year. Don Juan told him that the new history related how Don Quixote — whoever this Don Quixote might be — had competed there in a tilting at the ring, in a contest barren of invention, threadbare in its mottoes, beggarly in its costumes, though rich in stupidities.

“For that very reason,” said Don Quixote, “I will not set foot in Saragossa; and in that way I will expose this new historian’s lie to the whole world, and people will see that I am not the Don Quixote he writes about.”
“That is the wise course,” said Don Jeronimo; “and there are other jousts at Barcelona, where Señor Don Quixote may display his valor.”
“So I intend,” said Don Quixote; “and since it is now time, I beg your worships to give me leave to retire to bed, and to count and keep me among the number of your truest friends and servants.”
“Me too,” said Sancho; “I may turn out to be good for something.”

With that they said their farewells, and Don Quixote and Sancho withdrew to their room, leaving Don Juan and Don Jeronimo marveling at the mixture he made of good sense and madness, and fully convinced that these two, and not the pair their Aragonese author had described, were the genuine Don Quixote and Sancho. Don Quixote rose early, and took leave of his hosts by rapping on the partition of the other room. Sancho paid the landlord handsomely, and advised him either to promise less about the provisions of his inn or to keep it better provided.

title: Part 2, Chapter 60
paragraphs: What happened to Don Quixote on his way to Barcelona

The morning was fresh and promised a cool day when Don Quixote left the inn, first making sure to learn the most direct route to Barcelona that avoided Saragossa altogether — so determined was he to prove this new historian, who they said had slandered him, a liar. As it turned out, nothing worth setting down happened to him for six days, at the end of which, having strayed off the road, night overtook him in a grove of oaks or cork trees; on this particular point Cide Hamete is less exact than he usually is about everything else.

Master and servant got down from their mounts, and once they had settled themselves at the foot of the trees, Sancho — who had eaten a solid midday meal that day — slipped without any ceremony straight through the gates of sleep. But Don Quixote, kept awake by his thoughts far more than by hunger, could not shut his eyes, and his imagination wandered back and forth through a thousand places. One moment he seemed to be in the cave of Montesinos, watching Dulcinea, changed into a peasant girl, leap up and mount her she-ass; the next, the words of the sage Merlin were ringing in his ears, spelling out the conditions to be met and the labors to be performed for Dulcinea's disenchantment. He lost all patience when he thought of the laziness and lack of charity in his squire Sancho, who, as far as he could tell, had given himself only five lashes — a pitiful number, absurdly out of proportion to the enormous total still owed. The thought stirred up such irritation and anger in him that he reasoned the matter out this way: "If Alexander the Great cut the Gordian knot, declaring, 'Cutting amounts to the same thing as untying,' and that did not stop him from becoming supreme lord of all Asia, then exactly the same could happen now with Dulcinea's disenchantment if I whip Sancho against his will; for if the condition of the remedy is that Sancho must receive three thousand and some lashes, what difference does it make to me whether he delivers them himself or someone else delivers them, when the essential point is that he receive them, no matter what hand they come from?"

With this idea in mind he went over to Sancho, having first taken Rocinante's reins and arranged them so he could use them as a whip, and he began undoing the laces (the common opinion is that Sancho had only one, in front) that held up his breeches; but the moment he came near, Sancho woke up wide awake and shouted, "What's going on? Who's touching me and untrussing me?"

"It is I," said Don Quixote, "and I have come to make good your failings and to relieve my own torments; I have come to whip you, Sancho, and to pay off some part of the debt you took upon yourself. Dulcinea is perishing, you go on living without a care, and I am dying of deferred hope; so untruss yourself willingly, for my will is to give you, here in this lonely spot, at least two thousand lashes."

"Nothing doing," said Sancho; "let your worship keep still, or by the living God the deaf will hear us. The lashes I committed myself to have to be voluntary, not forced on me, and right now I have no inclination whatever to whip myself; it's enough that I give you my word to flog and flail myself whenever the mood takes me."

"It will not do to leave it to your good graces, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "because your heart is hard and, peasant though you are, your flesh is tender;" and all the while he kept straining and struggling to untie him.

Seeing this, Sancho got to his feet, closed with his master, gripped him with all his strength in his arms, hooked a heel behind his leg, and brought him down flat on his back; then, pressing his right knee on his chest, he pinned his hands in his own so that he could neither move nor draw breath.
"What is this, traitor!" cried Don Quixote. "You rebel against your master and natural lord? You raise your hand against the one who gives you your bread?"

"I neither unmake kings nor make them," said Sancho; "I'm only defending myself, and I'm my own lord. If your worship promises me to stay quiet and not try to whip me now, I'll let you go free and unhindered; if not —

Traitor and foe of Doña Sancha,
here on this spot you die."

Don Quixote gave his promise, and swore by the life of his thoughts not to touch so much as a thread of Sancho's clothes, and to leave the whipping entirely to his free choice and discretion, to be done whenever he felt like it.

Sancho got up and moved some distance away, but just as he was about to lean against another tree he felt something brush his head, and reaching up with his hands he found a pair of human feet, with shoes and stockings on them. Shaking with fear, he moved to another tree, where exactly the same thing happened, and he began yelling, calling on Don Quixote to come and protect him. Don Quixote came, asked what had happened and what he was frightened of, and Sancho answered that all the trees were full of men's feet and legs. Don Quixote felt them, guessed immediately what they were, and said to Sancho, "You have nothing to fear; these feet and legs you can feel but cannot see undoubtedly belong to outlaws and bandits who have been hanged from these trees, for the authorities in this region are in the habit of stringing them up twenty and thirty at a time when they catch them — which leads me to conclude that I must be close to Barcelona;" and it was exactly as he supposed: at first light they looked up and saw that the fruit hanging on those trees was the bodies of bandits.

By now day was breaking; and if the dead bandits had frightened them, their hearts were no less shaken by upwards of forty live ones, who suddenly surrounded them and ordered them, in Catalan, to stand still and wait until their captain arrived. Don Quixote was on foot, his horse unbridled, his lance propped against a tree — in short, utterly defenseless; so he judged it best to fold his arms, bow his head, and save himself for a better time and opportunity. The robbers hurried to ransack Dapple and left him nothing of all he carried in the saddlebags and the valise; and it was lucky for Sancho that the duke's crowns, and the ones he had brought from home, were in a money-belt he wore around his waist. Even so, these good people would have stripped him bare, and searched even between skin and flesh for anything hidden, if their captain had not arrived at that moment — a man who looked about thirty-four, strongly built, taller than average, with a stern expression and a dark complexion. He rode a powerful horse, wore a coat of mail, and carried at his sides four of the pistols they call petronels in that country. He saw that his squires (for that is what they call men in that trade) were about to plunder Sancho Panza, and he ordered them to stop; they obeyed instantly, and so the money-belt was spared. He was struck by the sight of the lance leaning against the tree, the shield on the ground, and Don Quixote in armor and downcast, with the saddest, most melancholy face that sadness itself could have composed; and going up to him he said, "Don't be so dejected, good man, for you have not fallen into the hands of some inhuman Busiris, but into those of Roque Guinart, which are more merciful than cruel."

"The cause of my dejection," Don Quixote answered, "is not that I have fallen into your hands, O valiant Roque, whose fame no limits on earth can contain, but that my carelessness was so great that your soldiers caught me with my horse unbridled, when by the rule of the knight-errantry I profess I am bound to live always on the alert, at every hour my own sentinel; for let me tell you, great Roque, if they had found me on my horse, with my lance and my shield, it would have been no easy matter for them to make me surrender, because I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, the man who has filled the whole world with his deeds."

Roque Guinart saw at once that Don Quixote's infirmity had more to do with madness than with bravado; and although he had occasionally heard him mentioned, he had never taken the stories about him for true, nor could he convince himself that such a humor could take command of a man's heart; so he was delighted to have met him, and to test at close range what he had heard of from a distance. He said to him, "Do not despair, valiant knight, and do not count the situation you find yourself in as some hostile stroke of fate; it may well be that through these stumbles your twisted fortune will straighten itself out, for heaven, by strange and roundabout ways that men can neither trace nor comprehend, lifts up the fallen and makes the poor rich."

Don Quixote was about to thank him when they heard behind them a noise like a whole troop of horses; it was, however, only one, and on it, riding at a furious pace, came a youth of about twenty, dressed in green damask trimmed with gold, in breeches and a loose jacket, a hat cocked up in the Walloon style, tight polished boots, gilt spurs, dagger and sword, a small musket in his hand, and a pair of pistols at his waist.

Roque turned his head at the sound and saw this handsome figure, who rode up and addressed him: "I have come looking for you, valiant Roque, hoping to find in you, if not a cure, then at least some relief in my misfortune; and so as not to keep you guessing — for I can see you don't recognize me — I will tell you who I am. I am Claudia Jeronima, daughter of Simon Forte, your good friend and the particular enemy of Clauquel Torrellas, who is your enemy too, since he belongs to the faction opposed to you. You know that this Torrellas has a son who is called — or at least was called, less than two hours ago — Don Vicente Torrellas. Well, to shorten the story of my misfortune, I will tell you in a few words what this young man has brought upon me. He saw me, he courted me, I listened to him, and behind my father's back I fell in love with him — for there is no woman, however secluded her life or however closely she is guarded, who will not find opportunities and to spare for pursuing her headlong desires. In short, he promised to be mine and I promised to be his, and matters went no further. Yesterday I learned that, forgetting what he owed me, he was going to marry another, and that this very morning he was going to be betrothed — news that staggered me and put an end to my patience. My father was away from home, so I was able to put on the outfit you see, and spurring my horse to a gallop I caught up with Don Vicente about a league from here; and without stopping to make reproaches or hear excuses I fired this musket at him, and these two pistols on top of it, and as far as I can judge I must have lodged more than two bullets in his body, opening doors through which my honor could walk out free, wrapped in his blood. I left him there in the hands of his servants, who neither dared nor were able to step in to defend him; and I have come to ask you for a safe-conduct into France, where I have relatives I can live with, and to beg you as well to protect my father, so that Don Vicente's many kinsmen do not dare to take their lawless revenge on him."

Roque, marveling at the gallant bearing, the spirit, the fine figure, and the adventure of the fair Claudia, said to her, "Come, señora, let us go and see whether your enemy is dead, and afterwards we will decide what is best for you." Don Quixote, who had been listening attentively to what Claudia said and to Roque Guinart's reply, exclaimed, "No one need take the trouble of defending this lady, for I take that upon myself. Give me my horse and my arms and wait for me here; I will go in search of this knight, and dead or alive I will make him keep the word he pledged to so much beauty."

"Nobody should doubt that for a moment," said Sancho, "because my master has a wonderful hand for matchmaking; only a few days ago he forced another man to marry, one who had also gone back on his promise to a maiden; and if it hadn't been for his persecutors the enchanters turning the man's true shape into a lackey's, that maiden wouldn't be one this very minute."

Roque, whose mind was on the fair Claudia's affair rather than on the words of master or man, did not hear them; and after ordering his squires to give back to Sancho everything they had stripped from Dapple, he directed them to withdraw to the place where they had spent the night, and then rode off with Claudia at full speed to look for the wounded or dead Don Vicente. They came to the spot where Claudia had overtaken him, but found nothing there except freshly spilled blood; casting their eyes around, however, they made out some people on the slope of a hill above, and concluded — rightly, as it turned out — that it was Don Vicente, being carried by his servants, alive or dead, either to have his wounds treated or to be buried. They hurried to catch up, and since the group was moving slowly, they did so with ease. They found Don Vicente in his servants' arms, begging them in a faint, broken voice to let him die there, because the pain of his wounds would not let him go any farther. Claudia and Roque flung themselves from their horses and went up to him; the servants were frightened by the sight of Roque, and Claudia was shaken by the sight of Don Vicente; going up to him, half tender and half severe, she took his hand and said, "If you had given me this hand as we agreed, you would never have come to this."

The wounded gentleman opened his nearly closed eyes, and recognizing Claudia he said, "I see plainly, beautiful and deceived lady, that it is you who have killed me — a punishment my feelings for you never earned or deserved, for never in thought or in deed did I intend to wrong you, nor could I have."
"Then it isn't true," said Claudia, "that this morning you were going to marry Leonora, the daughter of the rich Balvastro?"

"Certainly not," Don Vicente replied; "my evil fortune must have carried that report to you, so that jealousy would drive you to take my life; but to set your mind at rest about it, press my hands and take me for your husband, if you will. I have no better amends to offer you for the wrong you believe you have suffered at my hands."

Claudia pressed his hands, and her own heart was pressed so hard that she fell fainting on Don Vicente's bleeding breast, just as a death spasm seized him. Roque stood bewildered, not knowing what to do; the servants ran for water to sprinkle on their faces, brought some, and bathed them with it. Claudia came out of her faint, but Don Vicente did not come out of his paroxysm, for his life had reached its end. When Claudia saw this, and had made certain that her beloved husband no longer lived, she split the air with her sighs and made the heavens ring with her cries; she tore her hair and flung it to the winds, she struck her own face with her hands, and showed every sign of grief and anguish that could be imagined to rise from an afflicted heart. "Cruel, thoughtless woman!" she cried, "how easily you were moved to carry out so wicked a design! O raging force of jealousy, to what desperate ends you drive those who give you lodging in their hearts! O husband, whose unhappy fate in being mine has carried you from the marriage bed to the grave!"

So violent and so pitiful were Claudia's laments that they drew tears from Roque's eyes, unaccustomed as they were to shedding them on any occasion. The servants wept, Claudia fainted again and again, and the whole place seemed a field of sorrow and a dwelling of misfortune. In the end Roque Guinart told Don Vicente's servants to carry his body to his father's village, which was nearby, for burial. Claudia told Roque that she meant to enter a convent where an aunt of hers was abbess, intending to spend her life there in the company of a better and more everlasting bridegroom. He praised her holy resolution and offered to escort her wherever she wished, and to defend her father against Don Vicente's kinsmen and against the whole world if they tried to harm him. Claudia refused his company on any terms, thanked him for his offers as well as her grief allowed, and took her leave of him weeping. Don Vicente's servants bore his body away, and Roque went back to his men — and so ended the love of Claudia Jeronima. But is that any wonder, when the web of her pitiable story was woven by the invincible and merciless power of jealousy?

Roque Guinart found his squires where he had ordered them to be, and Don Quixote among them, mounted on Rocinante, delivering a speech in which he urged them to abandon a way of life so dangerous to the soul as well as to the body; but since most of them were Gascons, rough and lawless men, his sermon did not make much of an impression. When Roque rode up he asked Sancho whether his men had returned and handed back the valuables and jewels they had stripped from Dapple. Sancho said they had, except that three kerchiefs were missing that were worth three cities.
"What are you saying, man?" said one of the bystanders; "I've got them, and they aren't worth three reals."
"That is so," said Don Quixote; "but my squire values them at the price he names because of the person who gave them to me."

Roque Guinart ordered them returned at once; then, making his men line up, he had them bring out all the clothing, jewelry, and money they had taken since the last division of spoils; and after a quick appraisal, converting into cash whatever could not be divided, he split it among the whole company so fairly and so prudently that in not a single instance did he go an inch beyond or fall a point short of strict distributive justice.
When this was finished and everyone was left content, Roque remarked to Don Quixote, "If I didn't keep this scrupulous exactness with these men, there would be no living with them."
At this Sancho observed, "From what I've seen here, justice is such a fine thing that it has to be used even among the thieves themselves."

One of the squires heard this, and swung up the butt of his harquebus, and would no doubt have cracked Sancho's skull with it if Roque Guinart had not shouted at him to stop. Sancho was frightened half to death, and resolved not to open his lips again as long as he was among these people.

At that moment one or two of the squires who were posted as sentries along the roads, to watch who passed and report everything to their chief, came up and said, "Señor, not far from here, on the road to Barcelona, a large company of people is coming."
To which Roque answered, "Have you made out whether they're the kind who are looking for us, or the kind we're looking for?"
"The kind we're looking for," said the squire.
"Then off with you, all of you," said Roque, "and bring them to me here at once, without letting a single one of them slip away."

They obeyed, and Don Quixote, Sancho, and Roque, left alone, waited to see what the squires would bring in; and while they waited, Roque said to Don Quixote, "This life of ours must look strange to Señor Don Quixote — strange adventures, strange happenings, every one of them dangerous; and I don't wonder it looks so, because I have to admit, truthfully, that there is no way of living more restless or more anxious than ours. What drew me into it was a certain thirst for revenge, which has power enough to unsettle the calmest of hearts. By nature I am compassionate and well-meaning; but, as I say, the desire to avenge a wrong that was done to me so overturns all my better inclinations that I keep on in this life against everything my conscience tells me; and as one abyss calls to another, and one sin to the next, acts of revenge have linked themselves into a chain, so that I now carry not only my own but other men's as well. Yet God is pleased to grant that, though I see myself in the middle of this labyrinth of entanglements, I have not lost hope of getting out of it and reaching a safe harbor."

Don Quixote was astonished to hear Roque speak such sound and sensible words, for he had not imagined that among men whose trade was robbing, murdering, and waylaying travelers there could be anyone capable of a virtuous thought; and he replied, "Señor Roque, the beginning of health lies in knowing one's disease and in the patient's willingness to take the medicines the physician orders. You are sick, you know what is wrong with you, and heaven — or to speak more accurately, God, who is our physician — will give you medicines to cure you: medicines that heal little by little, not suddenly or by miracle. Besides, sinners with understanding stand nearer to amendment than fools do; and since your worship has shown good judgment in what you have said, all that remains is to keep up your courage and trust that the sickness of your conscience will be healed. And if you want to shorten the road and set yourself easily on the path of salvation, come with me, and I will teach you to be a knight-errant — a calling in which so many hardships and misadventures are met with that, taken as penances, they will land you in heaven in the blink of an eye."

Roque laughed at Don Quixote's counsel, and changing the subject he recounted the tragic story of Claudia Jeronima, which grieved Sancho deeply, for the girl's beauty, daring, and spirit had not struck him as at all amiss.

And now the squires sent out to take the prize returned, bringing with them two gentlemen on horseback, two pilgrims on foot, a coach full of women with about six servants attending them on foot and on horseback, and a couple of muleteers belonging to the gentlemen. The squires formed a circle around them, victors and vanquished alike keeping a deep silence, waiting for the great Roque Guinart to speak. He asked the gentlemen who they were, where they were going, and how much money they carried. "Señor," one of them answered, "we are two captains of Spanish infantry; our companies are at Naples, and we are on our way to embark on four galleys said to be at Barcelona under orders for Sicily; we carry some two or three hundred crowns, which by our reckoning makes us rich and content, since a soldier's poverty allows no larger treasure."

Roque put the same questions to the pilgrims that he had put to the captains, and was told they were going to take ship for Rome and that between them they might have about sixty reals. He also asked who was in the coach, where they were headed, and what money they carried, and one of the men on horseback answered, "In the coach is my lady Doña Guiomar de Quiñones, wife of the regent of the Vicaria at Naples, with her young daughter, a maid, and a duenna; we six servants attend her, and the money comes to six hundred crowns."

"So then," said Roque Guinart, "we have here nine hundred crowns and sixty reals; my soldiers must come to about sixty; work out how much falls to each of them, because I'm a poor arithmetician." When the robbers heard this they raised a shout: "Long live Roque Guinart, in spite of the lladres who seek his ruin!"

The captains' distress showed plainly on their faces, the regent's lady looked crestfallen, and the pilgrims took no pleasure at all in seeing their goods confiscated. Roque held them in suspense like this for a while; but he had no wish to drag out their misery, which could be seen from a bowshot away, and turning to the captains he said, "Sirs, will your worships be so courteous as to lend me sixty crowns, and her ladyship the regent's wife eighty, to satisfy this company that follows me — for 'the abbot must eat by his singing' — and then you may go on your way immediately, free and unhindered, with a safe-conduct I will give you, so that if you run into any other of my bands scattered through this country, they will do you no harm; for it is not my intention to wrong soldiers, or any woman, least of all one of rank."

Lavish and heartfelt were the thanks the captains paid Roque for his courtesy and generosity — for generosity is what they considered it, his leaving them their own money. Señora Doña Guiomar de Quiñones wanted to throw herself out of the coach to kiss the great Roque's feet and hands, but he would not allow it on any account; instead he begged her pardon for the wrong he had done her under the pressure of the harsh obligations of his unhappy calling. The regent's lady ordered one of her servants to hand over at once the eighty crowns assessed as her share, the captains having already paid out their sixty. The pilgrims were about to surrender their whole small store, but Roque told them to keep still, and turning to his men he said, "Of these crowns, two go to each man, and twenty are left over; let ten be given to these pilgrims, and the other ten to this good squire, so that he can speak well of this adventure;" and then, having writing materials brought — he always traveled with them — he gave them a written safe-conduct addressed to the leaders of his bands; and bidding them farewell, he let them go free, full of wonder at his nobility, his generous nature, and his unusual conduct, and inclined to look on him as an Alexander the Great rather than a notorious robber.

One of the squires muttered in his half-Gascon, half-Catalan speech, "This captain of ours is better suited to be a friar than a highwayman; if he wants to play the generous man again, let him do it with his own property and not with ours."

The unlucky fellow did not speak quietly enough to escape Roque's hearing; drawing his sword, Roque all but split his head in two, saying, "This is how I punish insolent loose tongues." They were all stunned, and not one of them dared say a word — such was the obedience they paid him. Roque then drew apart and wrote a letter to a friend of his in Barcelona, telling him that the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha, the knight-errant everyone was talking about, was with him, and was, he assured him, the funniest and most sensible man in the world; and that four days from then, on Saint John the Baptist's Day, he would set him down in the middle of the city's beach, in full armor, mounted on his horse Rocinante, with his squire Sancho on an ass; and he asked him to pass the news to his friends the Niarros, so they could amuse themselves with him. He wished, he said, that his enemies the Cadells could be cheated of that pleasure, but it was impossible, because Don Quixote's mad fits and shrewd sayings, and the drolleries of his squire Sancho Panza, could not fail to delight the whole world. He sent the letter off with one of his squires, who, swapping his highwayman's clothes for a peasant's, slipped into Barcelona and delivered it to the man it was addressed to.

title: Part 2, Chapter 61
paragraphs: What happened to Don Quixote when he entered Barcelona, together with other matters that lean more toward the true than the ingenious

Don Quixote spent three days and three nights with Roque, and if he had spent three hundred years he would still have found plenty to observe and marvel at in the way the man lived. At dawn they were in one place, by dinnertime in another; sometimes they fled without knowing who was after them, and at other times they lay in ambush without knowing for whom. They slept on their feet, interrupting their rest to move from spot to spot. The whole business was nothing but dispatching spies and scouts, posting sentinels, and keeping the matches of harquebuses lit—though they carried few of those, since nearly everyone used flintlocks. Roque spent his nights somewhere apart from his men so that they would never know where he was, because the many proclamations the viceroy of Barcelona had issued against his life kept him anxious and on edge, and he dared trust no one, fearing that even his own men might kill him or hand him over to the authorities—truly, a weary and miserable existence! At last, by unfrequented roads, shortcuts, and hidden paths, Roque, Don Quixote, and Sancho set out for Barcelona with six squires. They reached the beach on the night of Saint John's Eve, and Roque, after embracing Don Quixote and Sancho (and giving Sancho the ten crowns he had promised but never until then handed over), left them, with many warm expressions of goodwill exchanged on both sides.

Roque rode back, and Don Quixote stayed on horseback, just as he was, waiting for daylight. It was not long before the face of fair Aurora began to appear at the balconies of the east, cheering the grass and the flowers, if not the ear—though the ear was cheered too, for at that same moment there came a sound of clarions and drums, a clamor of bells, and the tramp, tramp of running feet with shouts of "Make way there! Clear the way!" apparently pouring out of the city.

Dawn gave way to the sun, which, with a face broader than a shield, began climbing slowly above the low line of the horizon. Don Quixote and Sancho looked all around them and saw the sea—a sight they had never laid eyes on before. It struck them as immensely vast and wide, far more so than the lakes of Ruidera they had seen in La Mancha. They saw the galleys drawn up along the shore, which, lowering their awnings, showed themselves decked out with streamers and pennants that fluttered in the breeze, kissing and sweeping the water, while aboard them bugles, trumpets, and clarions sounded, filling the air near and far with sweet, martial music. Then the galleys got under way and performed a kind of mock battle on the calm water, while a great crowd of horsemen on fine mounts and in splendid liveries rode out of the city and carried out a similar maneuver on their side. The soldiers on the galleys kept up a constant fire, answered by those on the city's walls and forts, and the heavy cannon split the air with their tremendous roar, to which the gangway guns of the galleys replied in turn. The shining sea, the smiling land, the clear air—though now and then darkened by gunsmoke—seemed to fill the whole crowd with a delight no one had expected. As for Sancho, he could not work out how those great hulks moving across the sea came to have so many feet.

And now the liveried horsemen came galloping up, with shouts and wild cries and cheers, to where Don Quixote stood astonished and wondering; and one of them—the one Roque had sent word to—called out to him, "Welcome to our city, mirror, beacon, star, and lodestar of all knight-errantry in its fullest extent! Welcome, I say, valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha—not the false one, the counterfeit, the apocryphal one that these recent days have served up to us in lying histories, but the true, the legitimate, the genuine one whom Cide Hamete Benengeli, the flower of historians, has described for us!"

Don Quixote made no reply, and the horsemen did not wait for one; wheeling around with all their followers, they began prancing in circles about Don Quixote, who turned to Sancho and said, "These gentlemen have clearly recognized us. I would bet they have read our history, and even that newly printed one by the Aragonese."

The cavalier who had spoken to Don Quixote rode up to him again and said, "Come with us, Señor Don Quixote, for we are all your servants and close friends of Roque Guinart"; to which Don Quixote answered, "If courtesy gives birth to courtesy, then yours, sir knight, is the daughter—or at least a near relative—of the great Roque's. Take me wherever you please; I shall have no will but yours, above all if you choose to put it to use in your service."

The cavalier answered with words just as gracious, and then, all of them closing in around him, they set off with him toward the city to the music of the clarions and drums. But as they were entering it, the evil one, who is the author of all mischief, and the boys, who are more mischievous than the evil one himself, arranged matters so that two of these bold, irrepressible urchins pushed their way through the crowd, and—one lifting Dapple's tail and the other Rocinante's—stuffed a bunch of furze under each. The poor animals felt these strange spurs, and by clamping their tails down tight they only made their torment worse, until, bucking and capering wildly, they pitched their riders to the ground. Don Quixote, mortified and thoroughly embarrassed, hurried to pull the plume from his poor nag's tail, while Sancho did the same for Dapple. Their escorts wanted to punish the boys for their insolence, but there was no chance of it, for the pair vanished among the hundreds of others trailing behind. Don Quixote and Sancho mounted again, and with the same music and the same acclamations they arrived at their escort's house, which was large and stately—the house, in short, of a wealthy gentleman; and there we will leave them for now, because such is Cide Hamete's pleasure.

title: Part 2, Chapter 62
paragraphs: Which recounts the adventure of the enchanted head, along with other trifling matters that cannot be left untold

Don Quixote's host was a man named Don Antonio Moreno, a gentleman of wealth and good sense who loved amusing himself in any decent, good-humored way; and now that he had Don Quixote under his roof, he began thinking up ways to draw out his madness without doing him any harm—for a joke that wounds is no joke at all, and no entertainment is worth having if it comes at someone else's expense. The first thing he did was have Don Quixote remove his armor and then parade him, in that snug chamois outfit we have already described and pictured more than once, out onto a balcony overlooking one of the city's main streets, in plain sight of the crowds and the boys, who stared at him as if he were a monkey on display. The riders in livery wheeled and pranced before him once again, as though they had put on their finery for him alone rather than to brighten that day's festival, and Sancho was beside himself with pleasure, because it seemed to him—he couldn't say how—that he had stumbled into another wedding like Camacho's, another house like Don Diego de Miranda's, another castle like the duke's. Several of Don Antonio's friends dined with him that day, and all of them paid honor to Don Quixote and treated him as a knight-errant, which so puffed him up and elevated him that he could hardly contain his satisfaction. As for Sancho, his witticisms were such that the entire household staff, and everyone else within earshot, hung on his every word. While they were at the table Don Antonio said to him, "We hear, good Sancho, that you are so fond of blancmange and meatballs that if any are left over, you tuck them into your shirt for the next day."

"No, señor, that's not true," said Sancho, "because I'm more tidy than greedy, and my master Don Quixote here knows perfectly well that the two of us are used to living for a week on a handful of acorns or walnuts. Of course, if it happens that somebody offers me a heifer, I come running with the halter—by which I mean, I eat what's put in front of me and take my chances as they come; but anyone who says I'm a sloppy eater or not clean about it, let me tell him he's got it wrong—and I'd put that more strongly if I didn't respect the honorable beards sitting at this table."

"Truly," said Don Quixote, "Sancho's restraint and cleanliness at the table deserve to be inscribed and engraved on plates of bronze, to be remembered forever in ages yet to come. It's true that when he's hungry there is a certain look of voracity about him, since he eats at a furious rate and chews with both sides of his jaw at once; but he never forgets his cleanliness, and during his time as governor he learned to eat with such delicacy that he takes his grapes, and even pomegranate seeds, with a fork."
"What!" said Don Antonio. "Sancho has been a governor?"

"Yes," said Sancho, "of an island called Barataria. I governed it to perfection for ten days, and lost my peace of mind the whole time, and learned to despise every government in the world. I got out of the place by running away, and fell into a pit where I gave myself up for dead, and only got out of it alive by a miracle."
Don Quixote then gave them a detailed account of the entire business of Sancho's governorship, which entertained his listeners enormously.

When the table was cleared, Don Antonio took Don Quixote by the hand and led him into a remote room whose only furnishing was a table, apparently of jasper, standing on a pedestal of the same material; on it was set a head, seemingly of bronze, in the style of the busts of the Roman emperors. Don Antonio walked Don Quixote through the whole apartment and circled the table with him several times, and then said, "Now, Señor Don Quixote, since I am satisfied that no one is listening and the door is shut, I am going to tell you about one of the rarest adventures—or rather, one of the strangest things—imaginable, on the condition that you keep what I say buried in the deepest vaults of secrecy."

"I swear it," said Don Quixote, "and for extra security I will lay a flagstone over it; for I would have you know, Señor Don Antonio" (by now he had learned his host's name), "that you are speaking to a man who has ears to hear but no tongue to tell, so you may safely pour whatever is in your breast into mine and trust that you have dropped it into the depths of silence itself."

"Trusting in that promise," said Don Antonio, "I will astonish you with what you are about to see and hear, and ease some of the frustration I feel at having no one to whom I can confide my secrets—for they are not the kind that can be trusted to just anyone."

Don Quixote was puzzled, wondering what could be the point of all these precautions; then Don Antonio took his hand and passed it over the bronze head and over the whole table and the jasper pedestal it stood on, and said, "This head, Señor Don Quixote, was made and constructed by one of the greatest magicians and sorcerers the world has ever known—a Pole by birth, I believe, and a pupil of the famous Escotillo about whom so many marvelous stories are told. He stayed here in my house, and for the sum of a thousand crowns that I paid him he built this head, which has the power and property of answering any question spoken into its ear. He plotted compass bearings, drew figures, studied the stars, watched for the favorable moments, and at last brought it to the perfection we shall witness tomorrow—for on Fridays it is mute, and since today is Friday we must wait until the next day. In the meantime your worship can think over what you would like to ask it; and I know from experience that everything it answers is the truth."

Don Quixote was astonished at the head's power and property, and was inclined not to believe Don Antonio; but seeing how little time he would have to wait before putting it to the test, he chose to say nothing except to thank him for revealing so great a secret. They then left the room, Don Antonio locked the door behind them, and they returned to the hall where the other gentlemen were gathered. In the meantime Sancho had been telling them about a number of the adventures and mishaps that had befallen his master.

That afternoon they took Don Quixote out for a ride, not in his armor but in town clothes, wearing a long coat of tawny cloth that, at that season, would have made ice itself break into a sweat. The servants were given orders to keep Sancho entertained so he wouldn't leave the house. Don Quixote rode not on Rocinante but on a tall, smooth-gaited mule with handsome trappings. They dressed him in the coat, and on his back, without his noticing, they pinned a parchment on which they had written in large letters, "This is Don Quixote of La Mancha." From the moment they set out, the sign drew the eyes of everyone who happened to pass, and as people read aloud, "This is Don Quixote of La Mancha," Don Quixote marveled that so many gazed at him, called him by name, and knew who he was; and turning to Don Antonio, who rode beside him, he remarked, "Great indeed are the privileges that come with knight-errantry, for it makes whoever practices it known and famous in every corner of the earth. Look, Don Antonio—even the very boys of this city know me, though they have never laid eyes on me before."

"True, Señor Don Quixote," replied Don Antonio, "for just as fire cannot be hidden or shut away, virtue cannot avoid being recognized; and the virtue won through the profession of arms shines out above every other kind."

But it so happened that as Don Quixote rode along amid all this acclaim, a Castilian who had read the sign on his back called out in a loud voice, "The devil take you for a Don Quixote of La Mancha! How is it you've made it this far without dying of the countless beatings that have rained down on your ribs? You are mad—and if you were mad in private and kept your madness to yourself, it would be less of an evil; but you have the knack of turning everyone who deals with you or talks with you into fools and blockheads. Just look at these gentlemen keeping you company! Go home, you idiot; look after your affairs, your wife, and your children, and give up this nonsense that's eating away your brain and skimming off your wits."

"Brother, go about your business," said Don Antonio, "and keep your advice for those who ask for it. Señor Don Quixote is entirely in his right mind, and we who accompany him are no fools; virtue deserves honor wherever it is found. Now be off with you, and bad luck go with you, and stop meddling where you're not wanted."

"By God, your worship is right," answered the Castilian, "because giving this good man advice is kicking against the goad; all the same, it makes me genuinely sad that the sound intelligence they say this blockhead has in every other matter should drain away down the channel of his knight-errantry. But may the bad luck your worship mentioned follow me and all my descendants if from this day forward—even if I live longer than Methuselah—I ever offer advice to anyone again, even if he begs me for it."

The advice-giver went on his way and the ride continued; but the crush of boys and townspeople pressing in to read the sign grew so great that Don Antonio had to take it off, pretending he was removing something else.

Night fell, they returned to the house, and there was a ladies' ball, for Don Antonio's wife—a woman of rank, high spirits, beauty, and wit—had invited some of her friends to come honor her guest and enjoy his extraordinary delusions. A good number came, they dined splendidly, and the dancing began at about ten o'clock. Among the ladies were two with a mischievous, playful streak who, while perfectly respectable, were rather free with their pranks when it came to harmless fun. These two were so relentless in dragging Don Quixote out to dance that they wore him down, not only in body but in spirit. He was a sight to behold—long, lank, lean, and sallow, his clothes plastered to his frame, awkward, and above all anything but light on his feet.

The merry ladies made sly advances to him, and he, just as slyly, rebuffed them; but finding himself hard pressed by their flirtations, he raised his voice and cried out, "_Fugite, partes adversæ!_ Leave me in peace, unwanted temptations! Away with your desires, ladies, for she who reigns as queen of mine, the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, allows no desires but her own to take me captive and bring me low." And with that he sat down on the floor in the middle of the room, worn out and shattered by all his exertions in the dance.

Don Antonio ordered him carried bodily to bed, and the first to take hold of him was Sancho, saying as he did so, "It was an unlucky hour when you took up dancing, master of mine. Do you suppose every strong man of valor is a dancer, or every knight-errant given to cutting capers? If you do, I can tell you you're mistaken—there's many a man who'd sooner take on a giant than attempt a caper. Now if it had been the heel-stomp you were trying, I could stand in for you, because I can do the heel-stomp like a gerfalcon; but at proper dancing I'm useless."

With these remarks and others like them, Sancho set the whole ballroom laughing, and then he put his master to bed, tucking him in well so he could sweat out whatever chill he might have caught from his dancing.

The next day Don Antonio decided it was time to try out the enchanted head; and so, with Don Quixote, Sancho, two friends of his, and the two ladies who had danced Don Quixote into exhaustion at the ball—they had spent the night with Don Antonio's wife—he shut himself into the room where the head stood. He explained to them the power it possessed, swore them to secrecy, and told them that this was the first time he was going to test the enchanted head's virtue. Apart from Don Antonio's two friends, no one else was in on the trick of the enchantment—and even they, had Don Antonio not let them in on it beforehand, would inevitably have been struck with the same amazement as everyone else, so cleverly and skillfully was the thing contrived.

The first to put his mouth to the head's ear was Don Antonio himself, who said in a low voice—but not so low that everyone couldn't hear—"Head, tell me, by the power that lives in you: what am I thinking at this moment?"
Without any movement of its lips, the head answered in a clear, distinct voice that everyone could hear, "I do not judge thoughts."

Everyone was dumbstruck at this, all the more because there was no one near the table or anywhere in the room who could have spoken the answer. "How many of us are here?" Don Antonio asked next, and the reply came in the same soft tone: "You and your wife are here, with two friends of yours and two of hers, and a famous knight called Don Quixote of La Mancha, and a squire of his named Sancho Panza."

Now the astonishment broke out afresh; now everyone's hair stood on end with awe; and Don Antonio, stepping back from the head, exclaimed, "This is enough to convince me that the man who sold you to me did not cheat me, O wise head, talking head, answering head, marvelous head! Let someone else come forward and ask it whatever they like."

And since women are generally quick to act and curious by nature, the first to step up was one of the two friends of Don Antonio's wife, and her question was, "Tell me, Head, what must I do to be very beautiful?" The answer she received was, "Be very modest."
"I have no further questions for you," said the fair questioner.

Her companion came up next and said, "I should like to know, Head, whether my husband loves me or not." The answer she was given was, "Consider how he treats you, and you may judge for yourself." The married lady withdrew, saying, "That answer hardly needed a question; obviously the treatment a person receives reveals the feelings of the one who gives it."

Then one of Don Antonio's two friends stepped forward and asked, "Who am I?" "You know," came the answer. "That isn't what I'm asking," said the gentleman; "I'm asking whether you know me." "Yes, I know you—you are Don Pedro Noriz," was the reply.

"I need to know no more," said the gentleman, "for this alone convinces me, O Head, that you know everything." As he withdrew, the other friend approached and asked, "Tell me, Head, what does my eldest son want?"
"I have said already," came the answer, "that I do not judge wishes; nevertheless, I can tell you that what your son wishes is to bury you."
"That," said the gentleman, "is a case of 'what I see with my eyes I point out with my finger'—so I'll ask nothing further."

Don Antonio's wife came forward and said, "I don't know what to ask you, Head; I only want to learn from you whether I shall enjoy my good husband for many years." And the answer given her was, "You shall, for his health and his temperate way of living promise him many years of life, which so many others cut short through excess."

Then Don Quixote stepped up and said, "Tell me, you who answer: was what I describe as having happened to me in the cave of Montesinos the truth, or a dream? Will Sancho's whipping be carried through to the end without fail? Will the disenchantment of Dulcinea come to pass?"

"As for the matter of the cave," came the reply, "there is much to be said—it has something of both in it. Sancho's whipping will go forward at a leisurely pace. The disenchantment of Dulcinea will reach its proper completion."
"That is all I wish to know," said Don Quixote. "Let me only see Dulcinea disenchanted, and I will count all the good fortune I could ever desire as having come to me at a single stroke."

The last to ask was Sancho, and his questions were these: "Head, will I by any chance get another government? Will I ever escape this hard life of a squire? Will I ever get back to see my wife and children?" The answer came: "You shall govern in your own house; and if you return to it, you shall see your wife and children; and when you stop serving, you shall stop being a squire."
"Good, by God!" said Sancho Panza. "I could have told myself that much—the prophet Perogrullo couldn't have put it better."
"What kind of answer did you expect, you brute?" said Don Quixote. "Isn't it enough that the replies this head gives fit the questions it's asked?"
"Yes, it's enough," said Sancho, "but I'd have liked it to speak more plainly and tell me more."

The questions and answers ended there, but not the wonder that filled everyone except Don Antonio's two friends, who knew the secret. That secret Cide Hamete Benengeli chose to reveal at once, so as not to keep the world in suspense imagining that the head held some strange magical mystery. He says that Don Antonio, copying another head he had seen in Madrid, the work of an image-maker, built this one at home for his own amusement and to astound the ignorant; and its mechanism worked as follows. The tabletop was wood, painted and varnished to look like jasper, and the pedestal supporting it was of the same material, with four eagles' claws projecting from it to carry the weight more securely. The head, which looked like the bust or likeness of a Roman emperor and was tinted the color of bronze, was hollow all the way through, as was the tabletop, into which it was fitted so precisely that no seam could be seen where they joined. The table's pedestal was hollow as well and connected with the throat and neck of the head, and the whole apparatus communicated with another room directly beneath the chamber where the head stood. Running through the entire cavity—pedestal, table, throat, and neck of the bust or figure—was a tin tube, carefully fitted and hidden from view. In the room below, matching the one above, sat the person who was to give the answers, his mouth pressed to the tube; and the voice traveled, as through an ear-trumpet, from above downward and from below upward, the words arriving clear and distinct, so that the trick was impossible to detect. The answerer was a nephew of Don Antonio's, a sharp, quick-witted student; and since his uncle had told him in advance who would be coming into the chamber with him that day, it was easy for him to answer the first question promptly and accurately. The rest he answered by guesswork—and, being clever, he guessed cleverly. Cide Hamete adds that this marvelous device remained in operation for some ten or twelve days; but as word spread through the city that Don Antonio had in his house an enchanted head that answered everyone who questioned it, he grew afraid the news might reach the ears of the vigilant sentinels of our faith, and so he explained the matter to the inquisitors, who ordered him to dismantle it and be done with it, lest the ignorant masses be scandalized. In the opinion of Don Quixote and Sancho, however, the head remained an enchanted one, fully capable of answering questions—rather more to Don Quixote's satisfaction than to Sancho's.

The gentlemen of the city, to please Don Antonio, to do the honors for Don Quixote, and to give him an occasion for displaying his folly, arranged a tilting at the ring to be held six days later—which, however, for a reason that will be explained in due course, never took place.

Don Quixote felt like exploring the city quietly and on foot, fearing that if he went on horseback the boys would chase after him; so he and Sancho, with two servants Don Antonio provided, set out for a walk. As it happened, going down one of the streets, Don Quixote looked up and saw written in very large letters over a doorway, "Books printed here," which delighted him greatly, for he had never before seen a printing house and was curious to know what one was like. He went in with his whole retinue and watched them pulling sheets in one place, correcting proofs in another, setting type here, revising there—in short, all the operations to be seen in a great printing house. He approached one of the cases and asked what was being done there; the workmen explained, he watched in wonder, and moved on. Among others, he came up to one man and asked him what he was working on. The workman answered, "Señor, this gentleman here" (and he pointed to a man of pleasing appearance and a certain gravity of manner) "has translated an Italian book into our Spanish tongue, and I am setting it in type for the press."
"What is the book's title?" asked Don Quixote; to which the author replied, "Señor, in Italian the book is called _Le Bagatelle_."
"And what does _Le Bagatelle_ mean in our Spanish?" asked Don Quixote.
"_Le Bagatelle_," said the author, "is as if we were to say in Spanish _Los Juguetes_; but though the book carries a humble name, it contains good solid substance."

"I have a small smattering of Italian myself," said Don Quixote, "and I pride myself on singing a few of Ariosto's stanzas; but tell me, señor—and I say this not to test your ability but purely out of curiosity—have you ever come across the word _pignatta_ in your book?"
"Yes, many times," said the author.
"And how do you render it in Spanish?"
"How else would I render it," replied the author, "than by _olla_?"

"Good heavens," exclaimed Don Quixote, "what a master you are of the Italian language! I would wager good money that where the Italian says _piace_ you put _place_ in Spanish, and where it says _piu_ you put _mas_, and that you translate _sù_ as _arriba_ and _giù_ as _abajo_."
"Of course that's how I translate them," said the author, "since those are their proper equivalents."

"I would dare to swear," said Don Quixote, "that your worship is unknown to the world, which always begrudges its rewards to rare talents and praiseworthy labors. What abilities lie wasted there! What genius shoved into corners! What worth left to molder! Even so, it seems to me that translating from one language into another, unless it be from the queens of languages, Greek and Latin, is like looking at Flemish tapestries from the wrong side: the figures are visible, but they are clouded by threads that obscure them, and they lack the smooth, bright finish of the right side. And translating from easy languages shows no more wit or command of words than copying or transcribing one document from another. By this I don't mean to suggest that the work of translating deserves no credit, for a man could occupy himself in worse ways and ones less profitable to him. I leave out of this reckoning two famous translators: Doctor Cristóbal de Figueroa with his _Pastor Fido_ and Don Juan de Jáuregui with his _Aminta_, where each achieves such felicity that one cannot tell which is the translation and which the original. But tell me—are you printing this book at your own expense, or have you sold the rights to some bookseller?"
"I print at my own risk," said the author, "and I expect to clear at least a thousand ducats on this first edition, which will run to two thousand copies and sell out in no time at six reals apiece."

"A fine piece of arithmetic!" said Don Quixote. "It's obvious you don't know the tricks of the printers and the way they play into one another's hands. I promise you, when you find yourself burdened with two thousand copies, your body will ache in ways that will astonish you—especially if the book is at all unusual and not the least bit spicy."

"What!" said the author. "Would your worship have me hand it over to a bookseller who'll pay three maravedis for the rights and think he's doing me a kindness? I don't print my books to win fame in the world—my works have already made me known in it. I want profit; without it, reputation isn't worth a farthing."

"God grant your worship good fortune," said Don Quixote; and he moved on to another case, where he saw them correcting a sheet of a book entitled "Light of the Soul." Taking note of it, he remarked, "Books like this one, plentiful as they are, are the books that deserve printing, for the sinners nowadays are many, and infinite lights are needed for so many who walk in darkness."

He walked on and saw that they were also correcting another book; and when he asked its title, they told him it was called "The Second Part of the Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha," by someone from Tordesillas.

"I've heard of this book already," said Don Quixote, "and truly, on my conscience, I thought it had been burned to ashes by now for its impertinence; but its Martinmas will come, as it comes to every pig. Invented stories are only as good and as delightful as they are close to the truth or the likeness of truth, and true ones are the better the truer they are." And so saying, with a flicker of irritation on his face, he walked out of the printing house. That same day Don Antonio arranged to take him to see the galleys anchored off the beach, which thrilled Sancho, who had never in his life seen any. Don Antonio sent word to the commandant of the galleys that he would be bringing his guest that afternoon—the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha, of whom the commandant and all the townspeople had already heard—to see them; and what happened aboard will be told in the following chapter.

title: Part 2, Chapter 63
paragraphs: About the mishap that befell Sancho Panza through his visit to the galleys, and the strange adventure of the fair Morisco

Don Quixote's thoughts ran deep on the enchanted head's reply, though none of them landed anywhere near the secret of the trick — all of them concentrated instead on the promise, which he treated as a certainty, of Dulcinea's disenchantment. He turned this over in his mind with great satisfaction, fully persuaded he would shortly see it come true; and as for Sancho, though, as has been said, he hated being a governor, he still had a hankering to give orders and be obeyed once more. This is the misfortune that comes with authority, even in jest.

To pick up the thread: that afternoon their host Don Antonio Moreno and his two friends, with Don Quixote and Sancho, went to the galleys. The commandant had already been told of his good fortune in seeing two such famous persons as Don Quixote and Sancho, and the instant they came to the shore all the galleys struck their awnings and the trumpets rang out. A skiff covered with rich carpets and crimson velvet cushions was lowered into the water, and as Don Quixote stepped on board the leading galley fired her gangway gun, and the other galleys did the same. As he mounted the starboard ladder the whole crew saluted him (as is the custom when a distinguished person comes on board a galley) by shouting "Hu, hu, hu," three times. The general — for so we shall call him, a Valencian gentleman of rank — gave him his hand, embraced him, and said, "I shall mark this day with a white stone as one of the happiest I can ever expect, since I have seen Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, the pattern and image in whom is contained and condensed all that is worthy in knight-errantry."

Don Quixote, delighted beyond measure with such a lordly reception, replied in words no less courteous. They all proceeded to the poop, which was handsomely decorated, and seated themselves on the bulwark benches. The boatswain went along the gangway and piped all hands to strip, which they did in an instant. Sancho, seeing so many men stripped to the skin, was taken aback, and even more so when he saw them spread the awning so briskly that it seemed to him all the devils were at work on it. But all this was cakes and fancy bread compared to what I am about to tell. Sancho was seated on the captain's stage, close to the aftermost rower on the right-hand side. He, briefed in advance on what to do, took hold of Sancho, hoisted him up in his arms, and the whole crew, who were standing ready, beginning on the right, passed him along, whirling him from hand to hand and bench to bench with such speed that it took the sight out of poor Sancho's eyes. He was quite sure the devils themselves were flying off with him. They did not leave off until they had sent him back along the left side and deposited him on the poop, and the poor man was left bruised, breathless, drenched in sweat, and unable to grasp what had just happened to him.

When Don Quixote saw Sancho's flight without wings, he asked the general whether this was a usual ceremony for newcomers on board the galleys; because, if so, since he had no intention of adopting it as a profession, he had no mind to perform such feats of agility, and if anyone tried to grab hold of him to whirl him about, he swore to God he would kick his soul out. As he said this he stood up and clapped his hand on his sword. Just then they struck the awning and lowered the yard with an enormous rattle. Sancho thought heaven was coming off its hinges and about to fall on his head, and in his terror he ducked it and buried it between his knees. Don Quixote's knees were not entirely under control either — he too shook a little, hunched his shoulders, and lost colour. The crew then hoisted the yard with the same speed and clatter, all the while keeping silence as if they had neither voice nor breath. The boatswain gave the signal to weigh anchor, and leaping onto the middle of the gangway began to lay on to the shoulders of the crew with his whip, and gradually hauled the ship out to sea.

When Sancho saw so many red feet (for that's what he took the oars to be) moving all together, he said to himself, "It's these that are the real enchanted things, not the ones my master goes on about. What can those wretches have done to be so whipped — and how does that one man strolling along whistling dare to whip so many? I declare, this is hell, or at the very least purgatory!"

Don Quixote, observing how attentively Sancho watched what was going on, said to him, "Ah, Sancho my friend, how quickly and cheaply you could finish off Dulcinea's disenchantment if you'd strip to the waist and take your place among those gentlemen!
