Surrounded by the pain and suffering of so many, you wouldn't feel your own much; and besides, perhaps the sage Merlin would allow each of these lashes, laid on with a good hand, to count for ten of the ones you must give yourself in the end."
The general was about to ask what these lashes were, and what Dulcinea's disenchantment was, when a sailor shouted, "Monjui signals that there is an oared vessel off the coast to the west."

On hearing this the general sprang onto the gangway crying, "Now then, my sons, don't let her give us the slip! It must be some Algerine corsair brigantine that the watchtower is signalling." The three other galleys immediately came alongside the chief galley for their orders. The general sent two out to sea while he kept inshore with the other, so the vessel could not escape. The crews plied the oars so furiously that the galleys seemed to fly. The two that had put out to sea, after a couple of miles, sighted a vessel which, as far as they could tell, they judged to be one of fourteen or fifteen banks of oars — and so she proved. As soon as the vessel spotted the galleys she went about, hoping to escape on her speed; but the attempt failed, for the chief galley was one of the fastest vessels afloat and overhauled her so quickly that those on board the brigantine saw there was no possibility of escape. The rais would have had them drop their oars and surrender so as not to provoke the captain in command. But chance ordered things otherwise. Just as the chief galley came close enough for those on board to hear the shouts calling on them to surrender, two Toraquis — that is to say two Turks — both drunk, who with a dozen more were on board the brigantine, fired their muskets and killed two of the soldiers lining the sides of our vessel. Seeing this the general swore he would not leave a single man alive among those on board, but as he bore down furiously on her she slipped out from under his oars. The galley shot well ahead; those on board the vessel saw their case was desperate, and while the galley was coming about they made sail, and by sailing and rowing tried once more to get away. Their effort did them less good than their rashness did them harm, for the galley caught up with them in a little more than half a mile, threw her oars over them, and took the whole crew alive. The other two galleys now joined company and all four returned with the prize to the beach, where a vast crowd stood waiting, eager to see what they had brought back. The general anchored close in, and saw that the viceroy of the city was on the shore. He ordered the skiff to push off to fetch him, and the yard to be lowered so as to hang at once the rais and the rest of the men taken on board the vessel — about thirty-six in number, all smart fellows and most of them Turkish musketeers. He asked which was the rais of the brigantine, and was answered in Spanish by one of the prisoners (who afterwards proved to be a Spanish renegade), "This young man, señor, that you see here is our rais," pointing to one of the handsomest and most gallant-looking youths imaginable. He did not look twenty years old.

"Tell me, dog," said the general, "what led you to kill my soldiers, when you saw it was impossible for you to escape? Is that how to behave to a chief galley? Don't you know that rashness is not valour? Faint prospects of success should make men bold, not reckless."

The rais was about to reply, but the general couldn't listen at that moment, as he had to hurry to receive the viceroy, who was now coming on board the galley with some of his attendants and some of the local people.
"You've had a good chase, señor general," said the viceroy.
"Your excellency shall soon see how good, by the game strung up to this yard," replied the general.
"How so?" asked the viceroy.

"Because," said the general, "against all law, reason, and the usages of war, they have killed on my hands two of the best soldiers on board these galleys, and I have sworn to hang every man I took — but above all this youth, who is the rais of the brigantine." And he pointed to him as he stood with his hands already bound and the rope around his neck, ready for death.

The viceroy looked at him, and seeing him so well-favoured, so graceful, and so submissive, felt a desire to spare his life — the youth's good looks acting at once as a letter of recommendation. He questioned him, saying, "Tell me, rais, are you Turk, Moor, or renegade?"
The youth replied, also in Spanish, "I am neither Turk, nor Moor, nor renegade."
"What are you, then?" said the viceroy.
"A Christian woman," replied the youth.
"A woman and a Christian, in such a dress and in such circumstances! That is more marvellous than credible," said the viceroy.
"Suspend the execution of the sentence," said the youth; "your vengeance will not lose much by waiting while I tell you the story of my life."

What heart could be so hard as not to soften at these words, at least enough to listen to what the unhappy youth had to say? The general told her to say what she pleased, but not to expect pardon for her flagrant offence. With this permission the youth began as follows.

"Born of Morisco parents, I am of that nation — more unhappy than wise — on which a sea of woes has lately poured down. In the course of our misfortunes I was carried off to Barbary by two uncles of mine, for it was useless to declare that I was a Christian, as in fact I am — and not a pretended or merely outward one, but a true Catholic Christian. It did me no good with those in charge of our sad expatriation to protest this, nor would my uncles believe it; on the contrary, they treated it as a lie and a ruse to let me stay behind in the land of my birth. And so, more by force than by my own will, they took me with them. I had a Christian mother, and a father who was a sensible man and a Christian too. I drank in the Catholic faith with my mother's milk, I was well brought up, and in neither word nor deed did I, I think, show any sign of being a Morisco. To match those virtues — for that is what I hold them to be — my beauty, if I have any, grew along with me; and great as was the seclusion in which I lived, it was not so great that a young gentleman, Don Gaspar Gregorio by name, eldest son of a gentleman who is lord of a village near ours, did not contrive to find opportunities of seeing me. How he saw me, how we met, how his heart was lost to me and mine not kept from him, would take too long to tell, especially at a moment when I am in dread of the cruel cord that threatens to come between my tongue and my throat. I will only say, therefore, that Don Gregorio chose to come with me into exile. He joined the Moriscoes who were going forth from other villages, for he knew their language well, and on the voyage he struck up a friendship with the two uncles who were carrying me with them. My father, as a wise and far-sighted man, had as soon as he heard the first edict for our expulsion left the village and gone in search of some refuge for us abroad. He left hidden and buried, at a spot known only to me, a large quantity of pearls and precious stones of great value, together with a sum of money in gold cruzadoes and doubloons. He charged me on no account to touch the treasure, if by any chance they expelled us before his return. I obeyed him, and with my uncles, as I have said, and others of our kindred and neighbours, crossed over to Barbary, and the place we ended up was Algiers — much the same as if we had ended up in hell itself. The king heard of my beauty, and rumour told him of my wealth, which was in some respects fortunate for me. He summoned me before him, and asked me what part of Spain I came from, and what money and jewels I had. I told him the place, and told him the jewels and money were buried there but could easily be recovered if I went back for them myself. All this I said, fearing my beauty rather than his own greed might influence him. While he was talking with me, they brought him word that one of the handsomest and most graceful youths imaginable was travelling in my company. I knew at once they were speaking of Don Gaspar Gregorio, whose looks outdid the most highly praised beauty. I was alarmed when I thought of the danger he was in, for among those barbarous Turks a fair youth is more prized than any woman, however beautiful. The king at once ordered him to be brought before him so he could see him, and asked me if what they said about the youth was true. Then, almost as if inspired by heaven, I told him it was — but that he should know it was not a man but a woman like myself, and I begged him to let me go and dress her in the attire proper to her, so her beauty could be seen to perfection and so she could present herself before him with less embarrassment. He told me to go by all means, and said that the next day we would discuss the plan for my return to Spain to carry away the hidden treasure. I went to Don Gaspar, told him the danger he was in if he let it be seen he was a man, dressed him as a Moorish woman, and that same afternoon brought him before the king, who was charmed at the sight of him, and resolved to keep the damsel and make a present of her to the Grand Signor. To avoid the risk she might run among the women of his harem, and distrustful of himself, he ordered her to be placed in the house of some Moorish ladies of rank who would protect and attend to her — and there he was taken at once. What we both suffered (for I cannot deny that I love him) can be left to the imagination of those who have been separated from someone they love dearly. The king then arranged that I should return to Spain in this brigantine, and that two Turks — the ones who killed your soldiers — should come with me. With me there also came this Spanish renegade" — and here she pointed to the one who had first spoken — "whom I know to be secretly a Christian, and more eager to be left in Spain than to return to Barbary. The rest of the crew of the brigantine are Moors and Turks, who only serve as rowers. The two Turks, greedy and insolent, instead of obeying the orders we had to put me and this renegade ashore in Christian dress (which we came supplied with) on the first Spanish ground we touched, chose to run along the coast and take some prize if they could, fearing that if they landed us first we might, if some accident happened to us, make it known the brigantine was at sea, and that, if there were any galleys on the coast, they might be caught. We sighted this shore last night, and knowing nothing of these galleys, were discovered — and the result is what you have seen. To sum up: there is Don Gregorio in woman's dress, among women, in imminent danger of his life; and here am I, hands bound, expecting — or rather dreading — to lose a life I am already weary of. Here, sirs, ends my sad story, as true as it is unhappy. All I ask of you is to let me die like a Christian, for, as I have already said, I am not to be charged with the offence of which those of my nation are guilty." And she stood silent, her eyes filled with moving tears, joined by plenty from the bystanders. The viceroy, touched with compassion, went up to her without speaking and untied the cord that bound the Moorish girl's hands.

But all the while the Morisco Christian was telling her strange story, an elderly pilgrim who had come on board the galley at the same time as the viceroy had kept his eyes fixed on her; and the instant she finished speaking he threw himself at her feet, embraced them, and said in a voice broken by sobs and sighs, "O Ana Felix, my unhappy daughter! I am your father Ricote, come back to look for you, unable to live without you, my soul!"

At these words Sancho opened his eyes and raised his head, which he had been holding down, brooding over his unlucky excursion; and looking at the pilgrim he recognised in him that same Ricote he had met the day he left his government, and was satisfied that this was his daughter. Now unbound, she embraced her father, mingling her tears with his, while he, addressing the general and the viceroy, said, "This, sirs, is my daughter, more unhappy in her adventures than in her name. She is Ana Felix, surnamed Ricote, as celebrated for her beauty as for my wealth. I quit my native land in search of some shelter or refuge for us abroad, and having found one in Germany I returned in this pilgrim's dress, in company with some other German pilgrims, to look for my daughter and take up a large quantity of treasure I had left buried. My daughter I did not find; the treasure I found and have with me; and now, in this strange roundabout way you have seen, I find the treasure that, more than all the rest, makes me rich — my beloved daughter. If our innocence, and her tears and mine, can with strict justice open the door to clemency, extend it to us, for we never had any intention of injuring you, nor do we sympathise with the aims of our people, who have been justly banished."

"I know Ricote well," said Sancho at this, "and I know too that what he says about Ana Felix being his daughter is true; but as for those other particulars about going and coming, and having good or bad intentions, I say nothing."

While everyone stood amazed at this strange turn of events, the general said, "At any rate your tears won't allow me to keep my oath. Live, fair Ana Felix, all the years that heaven has allotted you; but these rash, insolent fellows must pay the penalty of the crime they committed." And with that he gave orders to have the two Turks who had killed his two soldiers hanged at once from the yard-arm. The viceroy, however, begged him earnestly not to hang them, since their behaviour smacked more of madness than of bravado. The general yielded to the viceroy's request, for revenge is not easily taken in cold blood. They then tried to devise some scheme for rescuing Don Gaspar Gregorio from the danger he had been left in. Ricote offered for that purpose more than two thousand ducats he had in pearls and gems; they discussed several plans, but none so good as the one suggested by the renegade already mentioned, who offered to return to Algiers in a small vessel of about six banks, manned by Christian rowers, since he knew where, how, and when he could and should land, and knew the house where Don Gaspar was staying. The general and the viceroy had some hesitation about trusting the renegade with the Christians who were to row, but Ana Felix said she could vouch for him, and her father offered to go and pay the Christians' ransom if for some reason they did not come back. That being settled, the viceroy landed, and Don Antonio Moreno took the fair Morisco and her father home with him, the viceroy charging him to give them the best reception and welcome he could, while on his own part he offered everything his house contained for their entertainment — so great was the good will and kindness Ana Felix's beauty had infused into his heart.

title: Part 2, Chapter 64
paragraphs: About the adventure that gave Don Quixote more unhappiness than anything that had so far befallen him

Don Antonio Moreno's wife, so the history tells us, was extremely happy to see Ana Felix in her house. She welcomed her with great kindness, charmed by her beauty as much as by her intelligence — for in both respects the fair Morisco was richly endowed, and all the people of the city flocked to see her as though they had been summoned by the ringing of the bells.

Don Quixote told Don Antonio that the plan they had adopted for rescuing Don Gregorio was not a good one, since its risks were greater than its rewards, and it would be better for himself to land in Barbary with his arms and his horse; for he would carry him off in spite of the whole Moorish host, as Don Gaiferos carried off his wife Melisendra.

"Remember, your worship," Sancho observed on hearing him say this, "Señor Don Gaiferos carried off his wife from the mainland and took her to France by land; but in this case, if by chance we carry off Don Gregorio, we have no way of getting him to Spain — because there's the sea in between."
"There's a remedy for everything except death," said Don Quixote; "if they bring the vessel close to the shore we'll be able to get on board, though all the world try to prevent us."

"Your worship hits it off mightily well and mightily easy," said Sancho; "but 'it's a long step from saying to doing,' and I stick with the renegade, for he seems to me an honest, good-hearted fellow."

Don Antonio then said that if the renegade did not succeed, the alternative of the great Don Quixote's expedition to Barbary would be adopted. Two days later the renegade put to sea in a light vessel of six oars a side manned by a stout crew, and two days after that the galleys made sail eastward — the general having asked the viceroy to let him know all about the release of Don Gregorio and about Ana Felix, and the viceroy promised to do so.

One morning as Don Quixote went out for a stroll along the beach in full armour (for, as he often said, that was "his only gear, his only rest the fray," and he was never without it for a moment), he saw coming towards him a knight, also in full armour, with a shining moon painted on his shield. When the knight had come near enough to be heard, he said in a loud voice, addressing Don Quixote, "Illustrious knight, never sufficiently extolled Don Quixote of La Mancha, I am the Knight of the White Moon, whose unheard-of achievements will perhaps have recalled me to your memory. I have come to do battle with you and prove the might of your arm, with the aim of making you acknowledge and confess that my lady, whoever she may be, is incomparably fairer than your Dulcinea del Toboso. If you acknowledge this fairly and openly, you shall escape death and save me the trouble of inflicting it on you. If you fight and I defeat you, I demand no other satisfaction than this: that you lay aside your arms, give up going in quest of adventures, withdraw, and retire to your own village for the space of a year, to live there without putting hand to sword, in peace and quiet and beneficial repose, the same being needful for the increase of your estate and the salvation of your soul; and if you defeat me, my head shall be at your disposal, my arms and horse your spoils, and the renown of my deeds transferred and added to yours. Consider which will be your best course, and give me your answer quickly, for this day is all the time I have for the business."

Don Quixote was amazed and astonished both at the Knight of the White Moon's arrogance and at his reason for delivering the challenge, and with calm dignity he answered him, "Knight of the White Moon, of whose achievements I have never heard until now, I would venture to swear you have never seen the illustrious Dulcinea; for had you seen her, I know you would have taken care not to risk yourself on this issue, because the sight would have removed all doubt from your mind that there ever has been or could be a beauty to compare with hers. So, not saying you lie, but only that you are mistaken in what you state, I accept your challenge on the conditions you have proposed, and at once — so that the day you have set does not run out. From your conditions I except only that of the renown of your deeds being transferred to me, since I know nothing of what sort they are or what they may amount to; I am content with my own, such as they may be. So take whichever side of the field you prefer, and I will do the same; and whichever of us God grants the victory, may Saint Peter add his blessing."

The Knight of the White Moon had been seen from the city, and word was sent to the viceroy that he was in conversation with Don Quixote. The viceroy, supposing it must be some fresh prank arranged by Don Antonio Moreno or some other gentleman of the city, hurried out at once to the beach with Don Antonio and several other gentlemen, just as Don Quixote was wheeling Rocinante round to take up the necessary distance. The viceroy, seeing that the pair were clearly preparing to charge, put himself between them and asked what had led them to engage in combat so suddenly. The Knight of the White Moon replied that it was a question of precedence in beauty, and briefly told him what he had said to Don Quixote, and how the conditions of the challenge had been accepted on both sides. The viceroy went over to Don Antonio and asked in a low voice whether he knew who the Knight of the White Moon was, or whether it was some joke they were playing on Don Quixote. Don Antonio replied that he neither knew who he was nor whether the challenge was in joke or in earnest. This answer left the viceroy unsure whether he ought to let the combat go on or not; but unable to persuade himself that it was anything but a joke, he fell back, saying, "If there is no other way out of this, gallant knights, except to confess or die, and Don Quixote is inflexible, and your worship of the White Moon still more so, then in God's hand be it — fall on."

The Knight of the White Moon thanked the viceroy in courteous and well-chosen words for the permission he gave them, and so did Don Quixote, who then, commending himself with all his heart to heaven and to his Dulcinea, as was his custom on the eve of any combat, proceeded to take a little more distance, since he saw his opponent was doing the same. Then, without trumpet blast or any other warlike instrument giving them the signal to charge, both at the same instant wheeled their horses; and the Knight of the White Moon, being the swifter, met Don Quixote two-thirds of the way through the course and there encountered him with such violence that, without touching him with his lance (which he held high, evidently on purpose), he hurled Don Quixote and Rocinante to the ground — a perilous fall. He sprang on him at once, and placing the lance over his visor said to him, "You are vanquished, sir knight — nay, dead, unless you admit the conditions of our challenge."

Don Quixote, bruised and stunned, without raising his visor, said in a weak feeble voice, as if he were speaking out of a tomb, "Dulcinea del Toboso is the fairest woman in the world, and I the most unfortunate knight on earth; it is not fitting that this truth should suffer for my weakness. Drive your lance home, sir knight, and take my life, since you have taken away my honour."

"That I will not, truly," said the Knight of the White Moon; "let the fame of the lady Dulcinea's beauty live on undimmed. All I require is that the great Don Quixote retire to his own home for a year, or for as long a time as I shall enjoin upon him, as we agreed before engaging in this combat."

The viceroy, Don Antonio, and several others who were present heard all this, and heard too how Don Quixote replied that so long as nothing in prejudice of Dulcinea was demanded of him, he would observe all the rest like a true and loyal knight. With that pledge given, the Knight of the White Moon wheeled about, bowed his head to the viceroy, and rode away into the city at a half gallop. The viceroy told Don Antonio to hurry after him and find out by some means or other who he was. They lifted Don Quixote up and uncovered his face, finding him pale and bathed in sweat.

Rocinante, from the hard treatment he had received, lay unable to stir for the moment. Sancho, wholly dejected and woebegone, did not know what to say or do. He fancied that all of this was a dream, that the whole business was a piece of enchantment. Here was his master defeated, and bound not to take up arms for a year. He saw the light of the glory of his achievements darkened, and the hopes of the recent promises swept away like smoke before the wind; Rocinante, he feared, was crippled for life, and his master's bones out of joint — and if he were only shaken out of his madness, that would be no small luck. In the end they carried him into the city in a hand-chair which the viceroy sent for, and the viceroy himself returned too, eager to find out who this Knight of the White Moon was who had left Don Quixote in such a sad plight.

title: Part 2, Chapter 65
paragraphs: In which is made known who the Knight of the White Moon was; together with Don Gregorio's release, and other events

Don Antonio Moreno followed the Knight of the White Moon, and a number of boys followed him too — nay, pursued him — until they had him safely housed in a hostel in the heart of the city. Don Antonio, eager to make his acquaintance, went in too. A squire came out to meet him and remove his armour, and he shut himself into a lower room, still accompanied by Don Antonio, whose bread would not bake until he had found out who he was. The Knight of the White Moon, seeing that the gentleman would not leave him, said, "I know very well, señor, what you have come for: to find out who I am; and since there is no reason why I should conceal it from you, while my servant here is taking off my armour I will tell you the true state of the case, leaving nothing out. You must know, señor, that I am called the bachelor Samson Carrasco. I am from the same village as Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose craze and folly make all of us who know him feel pity for him — and I am one of those who have felt it most. Persuaded that his chance of recovery lay in quiet and in staying at home, I hit upon a scheme for keeping him there. Three months ago, therefore, I went out to meet him as a knight-errant under the assumed name of the Knight of the Mirrors, intending to engage him in combat and overcome him without hurting him, making it the condition of our combat that the loser should be at the victor's disposal. What I meant to demand of him (for I considered him already vanquished) was that he should return to his own village and not leave it for a whole year, by which time he might be cured. But fate ordered it otherwise: he defeated me and unhorsed me, and so my plan failed. He went on his way and I came back conquered, covered with shame, and badly bruised from my fall, which was particularly dangerous. But this did not quench my desire to meet him again and overcome him, as you have seen today. And since he is so scrupulous in observing the laws of knight-errantry, he will no doubt, in order to keep his word, obey the injunction I have laid on him. That, señor, is how the matter stands, and I have nothing more to tell you. I implore you not to betray me, or tell Don Quixote who I am; so that my honest efforts may succeed, and a man of excellent wits — were he only rid of the fooleries of chivalry — may get them back again."

"Oh señor," said Don Antonio, "may God forgive you the wrong you have done the whole world in trying to bring the most amusing madman in it back to his senses. Don't you see, señor, that the gain by Don Quixote's sanity can never equal the enjoyment his crazes give? But my belief is that all the señor bachelor's pains will be of no use in bringing a man so hopelessly cracked back to his senses; and if it weren't uncharitable, I would say may Don Quixote never be cured, for by his recovery we lose not only his own drolleries but his squire Sancho Panza's too — any one of which is enough to turn melancholy itself into merriment. However, I'll hold my peace and say nothing to him, and we'll see whether I am right in my suspicion that Señor Carrasco's efforts will be fruitless."

The bachelor replied that at any rate the affair was looking up, and he hoped for a happy result; and putting his services at Don Antonio's command, he took his leave. Having had his armour packed at once onto a mule, he rode away from the city that same day on the horse he had ridden into battle, and returned to his own country without any adventure worth recording in this truthful history.

Don Antonio reported to the viceroy what Carrasco had told him, and the viceroy was not very pleased to hear it, for with Don Quixote's retirement, the amusement of everyone who knew anything of his mad doings was at an end.

For six days Don Quixote kept to his bed, dejected, melancholy, moody and out of sorts, brooding over the unhappy event of his defeat. Sancho tried to comfort him, and among other things said to him, "Hold up your head, señor, and be of good cheer if you can, and give thanks to heaven that if you've had a tumble to the ground you haven't come off with a broken rib; and, as you know, 'where they give they take,' and 'there are not always fletches where there are pegs,' a fig for the doctor — there's no need of him to cure this ailment. Let's go home, and give up wandering about in search of adventures in strange lands and places. Properly looked at, I'm the greater loser, though it's your worship that has had the worse usage. With the government I gave up all wish to be a governor again, but I did not give up all longing to be a count — and that will never come to pass if your worship gives up becoming a king by renouncing the calling of chivalry; and so my hopes are going to turn into smoke."

"Peace, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "you see that my suspension and retirement are not to exceed a year. I shall soon return to my honoured calling, and I shall not be at a loss for a kingdom to win and a county to bestow on you."
"May God hear it and sin be deaf," said Sancho; "I have always heard say that 'a good hope is better than a bad holding.'"

As they were talking, Don Antonio came in looking extremely pleased and exclaiming, "Reward me for my good news, Señor Don Quixote! Don Gregorio and the renegade who went for him have come ashore — ashore do I say? They are by this time at the viceroy's house, and will be here in a moment."

Don Quixote cheered up a little and said, "Truly, I am almost ready to say I should have been glad if it had turned out just the other way, for it would have obliged me to cross over to Barbary, where by the might of my arm I should have restored to liberty not only Don Gregorio but all the Christian captives there are in Barbary. But what am I saying, miserable creature that I am? Am I not the one who has been defeated? Am I not he who has been overthrown? Am I not he who must not take up arms for a year? Then why am I making professions? What am I bragging about, when it is fitter for me to handle the distaff than the sword?"

"No more of that, señor," said Sancho; "'let the hen live, even if it be with her pip;' 'today for you and tomorrow for me;' in these matters of encounters and whacks one mustn't mind them, for he who falls today may get up tomorrow — unless he chooses to lie in bed, I mean gives in to weakness and doesn't pluck up fresh spirit for fresh battles. Let your worship get up now and receive Don Gregorio; the household seems to be in a bustle, and no doubt he's here by now." And so it proved, for as soon as Don Gregorio and the renegade had given the viceroy an account of the voyage out and home, Don Gregorio, eager to see Ana Felix, came with the renegade to Don Antonio's house. When they carried him off from Algiers he was in woman's dress; on board the vessel, however, he had exchanged it for that of a captive who escaped with him. But whatever dress he wore he looked like one to be loved and served and admired, for he was strikingly handsome, and to judge by appearances about seventeen or eighteen years old. Ricote and his daughter came out to welcome him — the father with tears, the daughter with bashfulness. They did not embrace, for where there is deep love there will never be overmuch boldness. Seen side by side, the handsomeness of Don Gregorio and the beauty of Ana Felix were the wonder of everyone present. It was silence that spoke for the lovers at that moment, and their eyes were the tongues that declared their pure and happy feelings. The renegade explained the measures and means he had used to rescue Don Gregorio, and Don Gregorio, at no great length but in a few words that showed his intelligence ran ahead of his years, described the peril and embarrassment he had found himself in among the women he had been staying with. In short, Ricote liberally rewarded both the renegade and the men who had rowed; and the renegade effected his readmission into the Church and was reconciled with it — from a rotten limb becoming, by penance and repentance, a clean and sound one.

Two days later the viceroy discussed with Don Antonio the steps they should take to enable Ana Felix and her father to stay in Spain, for it seemed to them there could be no objection to a daughter who was so good a Christian and a father so well disposed in appearance remaining there. Don Antonio offered to arrange the matter at the capital, where he was compelled to go on some other business, hinting that many a difficult affair was settled there with the help of favour and bribes.

"No," said Ricote, who was present during the conversation, "it will not do to rely on favour or bribes, because with the great Don Bernardino de Velasco, Conde de Salazar, to whom his Majesty has entrusted our expulsion, neither pleas nor promises, bribes nor appeals to compassion, are of any use. Though it is true he mixes mercy with justice, still, seeing that the whole body of our nation is tainted and corrupt, he applies to it the cautery that burns rather than the salve that soothes. Through prudence, sagacity, care, and the fear he inspires, he has borne on his mighty shoulders the weight of this great policy and carried it into effect, all our schemes and plots, importunities and wiles, being useless to blind his Argus eyes, ever on the watch lest one of us should remain behind in concealment — and like a hidden root, in time, sprout and bear poisonous fruit in a Spain now cleansed and relieved of the fear in which our vast numbers held it. A heroic resolve on the part of the great Philip the Third, and unparalleled wisdom to have entrusted it to the said Don Bernardino de Velasco!"

"At any rate," said Don Antonio, "when I am there I will make every possible effort, and let heaven do as pleases it best. Don Gregorio will come with me to relieve the anxiety his parents must be suffering over his absence; Ana Felix will stay in my house with my wife, or in a monastery; and I know the viceroy will be glad that the worthy Ricote should stay with him until we see what terms I can make."

The viceroy agreed to all that was proposed; but Don Gregorio, on learning what had been arranged, declared he could not and would not on any account leave Ana Felix. However, since it was his purpose to go and see his parents and devise some way of returning for her, he fell in with the proposed arrangement. Ana Felix stayed with Don Antonio's wife, and Ricote in the viceroy's house.

The day for Don Antonio's departure came; and two days later that for Don Quixote's and Sancho's, since Don Quixote's fall did not let him take the road sooner. There were tears and sighs, swoonings and sobs, at the parting between Don Gregorio and Ana Felix. Ricote offered Don Gregorio a thousand crowns if he would have them, but he would not take any save five, which Don Antonio lent him and he promised to repay at the capital. So the two of them took their departure, and Don Quixote and Sancho afterwards, as has already been said — Don Quixote without his armour and in travelling gear, and Sancho on foot, Dapple being loaded with the armour.

title: Part 2, Chapter 66
paragraphs: Which treats of what the reader will see, or what the listener will hear

As he left Barcelona, Don Quixote turned his gaze upon the spot where he had fallen. "Here Troy was," he said; "here my ill-luck, not my cowardice, robbed me of all the glory I had won; here Fortune made me the victim of her caprices; here the lustre of my achievements was dimmed; here, in a word, fell my happiness, never to rise again."

"Señor," said Sancho on hearing this, "it is the part of brave hearts to be patient in adversity just as much as to be glad in prosperity. I judge by myself: when I was a governor I was glad, and now that I am a squire and on foot I am not sad. And I have heard say that she whom people commonly call Fortune is a drunken whimsical jade, and, what is more, blind, and therefore neither sees what she does nor knows whom she casts down or whom she sets up."

"You are quite a philosopher, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "you speak very sensibly; I don't know who taught you. But I can tell you there is no such thing as Fortune in the world, nor does anything that takes place here, good or bad, come about by chance, but by the special preordination of heaven; and hence the common saying that 'each of us is the maker of his own Fortune.' I have been the maker of mine; but not with the proper amount of prudence, and my self-confidence has therefore made me pay dearly; for I should have reflected that Rocinante's feeble strength could not stand up to the mighty bulk of the Knight of the White Moon's horse. In a word, I ventured it, I did my best, I was overthrown — but though I lost my honour, I did not lose, nor can I lose, the virtue of keeping my word. When I was a knight-errant, daring and valiant, I backed my achievements by hand and deed; now that I am a humble squire I'll back my words by keeping the promise I have given. Forward then, Sancho my friend — let's go and keep the year of the novitiate in our own country, and in that seclusion we'll pick up fresh strength to return to my never-forgotten calling of arms."

"Señor," replied Sancho, "travelling on foot is not such a pleasant thing that it makes me feel disposed or tempted to make long marches. Let's leave this armour hung up on some tree, instead of somebody that's been hanged; and then with me on Dapple's back and my feet off the ground we'll arrange the stages as your worship pleases to measure them out. But to suppose I'm going to travel on foot, and make long stages at that, is to suppose nonsense."
"You say well, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "let my armour be hung up as a trophy, and under or around it we will carve on the trees what was inscribed on the trophy of Roland's armour —
_These let none move / Who dareth not his might with Roland prove._"
"That's the very thing," said Sancho; "and if it weren't that we should feel the want of Rocinante on the road, it would be just as well to leave him hung up too."
"And yet I'd rather not have either him or the armour hung up," said Don Quixote, "so it won't be said, 'for good service, a bad return.'"

"Your worship is right," said Sancho; "for, as sensible people hold, 'the fault of the ass must not be laid on the pack-saddle;' and since in this affair the fault is your worship's, punish yourself and don't let your anger break out against the already battered and bloody armour, or the meekness of Rocinante, or the tenderness of my feet, trying to make them travel more than is reasonable."

In conversation of this sort the whole of that day went by, as did the four following ones, without anything happening to interrupt their journey. But on the fifth, as they entered a village, they found a great many people at the door of an inn enjoying themselves, since it was a holiday. As Don Quixote approached, a peasant called out, "One of these two gentlemen who come here, and who don't know the parties, will tell us what we ought to do about our wager."
"That I will, certainly," said Don Quixote, "and according to the rights of the case, if I can manage to understand it."

"Well, here it is, worthy sir," said the peasant. "A man of this village who's so fat that he weighs twenty stone has challenged another, a neighbour of his, who weighs no more than nine, to run a race. The agreement was that they were to run a hundred paces with equal weights; and when the challenger was asked how the weights were to be equalised, he said that the other, weighing nine stone, should put eleven stone of iron on his back, so that the twenty stone of the thin man would equal the twenty stone of the fat one."

"Not at all," Sancho exclaimed at once, before Don Quixote could answer; "it's for me, who only a few days ago left off being a governor and a judge, as all the world knows, to settle these doubtful questions and give an opinion in disputes of every sort."
"Answer in God's name, Sancho my friend," said Don Quixote, "for I am not fit to give crumbs to a cat — my wits are so confused and upset."

With this permission, Sancho said to the peasants who stood clustered round him, waiting open-mouthed for the verdict, "Brothers, what the fat man is asking is not reasonable, nor has it a shadow of justice in it; because if it's true, as they say, that the challenged party may choose the weapons, the other has no right to choose ones that will prevent him from winning. My ruling, therefore, is this: that the fat challenger prune, peel, thin, trim, and correct himself, and take eleven stone of flesh off his body, here or there as he pleases and as suits him best; reduced in that way to nine stone weight, he'll make himself equal and even with his opponent's nine stone, and they'll be able to run on equal terms."

"By all that's good," said one of the peasants on hearing Sancho's decision, "the gentleman has spoken like a saint, and given judgment like a canon! But I'll bet the fat man won't part with an ounce of his flesh, let alone eleven stone."

"The best plan will be for them not to run," said another, "so that neither the thin man breaks down under the weight nor the fat one has to strip himself of his flesh. Let half the wager be spent on wine, and let's take these gentlemen to the tavern where there's the best, and 'over me be the cloak when it rains.'"

"I thank you, sirs," said Don Quixote, "but I can't stop for an instant, for sad thoughts and unhappy circumstances oblige me to seem discourteous and to travel fast." Spurring Rocinante, he pushed on, leaving them wondering at what they had seen and heard, at his own strange figure, and at the shrewdness of his servant — for such they took Sancho to be. Another of them observed, "If the servant is so clever, what must the master be? I'll bet, if they're going to Salamanca to study, they'll be alcaldes of the Court in no time; for it's a mere joke — only to read and read, have interest and good luck, and before a man knows where he is he finds himself with a staff in his hand or a mitre on his head."

That night master and man passed out in the open fields, and the next day, as they were continuing their journey, they saw coming towards them a man on foot with alforjas at his neck and a javelin or spiked staff in his hand — the very cut of a foot courier. As soon as he came close to Don Quixote he picked up his pace and, half running, came up to him, embraced his right thigh (for he could reach no higher), and exclaimed with evident pleasure, "O Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, what happiness it will be to my lord the duke's heart when he learns your worship is coming back to his castle — for he's still there with my lady the duchess!"
"I don't recognise you, friend," said Don Quixote, "and I don't know who you are unless you tell me."
"I am Tosilos, my lord the duke's lackey, Señor Don Quixote," replied the courier; "the one who refused to fight your worship about marrying the daughter of Doña Rodriguez."
"God bless me!" exclaimed Don Quixote; "is it possible you are the one whom my enemies the enchanters changed into the lackey you speak of, to rob me of the honour of that battle?"

"Nonsense, good sir!" said the messenger; "there was no enchantment or transformation at all. I entered the lists as lackey Tosilos and came out of them as lackey Tosilos. I thought I'd marry without fighting, since the girl had taken my fancy; but my scheme had a very different outcome, for as soon as your worship had left the castle my lord the duke had a hundred strokes of the stick given me for having gone against the orders he gave me before the combat. The upshot of the whole affair is that the girl has become a nun, Doña Rodriguez has gone back to Castile, and I'm now on my way to Barcelona with a packet of letters for the viceroy which my master is sending him. If your worship would like a drop, sound though warm, I have a gourd here full of the best, and some scraps of Tronchon cheese that'll serve as a provocative and wakener of your thirst if it happens to be asleep."
"I take the offer," said Sancho; "no more compliments about it; pour out, good Tosilos, in spite of all the enchanters in the Indies."

"You are indeed the greatest glutton in the world, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and the greatest fool on earth, not to be able to see that this courier is enchanted and this Tosilos a sham one. Stop with him and take your fill; I will go on slowly and wait for you to catch up."

The lackey laughed, unsheathed his gourd, unwalletted his scraps, and taking out a small loaf of bread, he and Sancho seated themselves on the green grass and in peace and good fellowship finished off the contents of the alforjas down to the bottom — so resolutely that they licked the wrapper of the letters, just because it smelt of cheese.
Said Tosilos to Sancho, "There's no doubt about it, Sancho my friend, this master of yours ought to be a madman."

"Ought!" said Sancho; "he owes no man anything; he pays for everything, especially when the coin is madness. I see it plain enough, and I tell him so plain enough; but what's the use? — especially now that it's all over with him, for here he is beaten by the Knight of the White Moon."

Tosilos begged him to explain what had happened, but Sancho replied that it wouldn't be good manners to leave his master waiting; some other day, if they met, there would be time enough for that. Then, getting up, after shaking out his doublet and brushing the crumbs out of his beard, he drove Dapple on before him, and saying goodbye to Tosilos, left him and rejoined his master, who was waiting for him under the shade of a tree.

title: Part 2, Chapter 67
paragraphs: About the resolution Don Quixote formed to turn shepherd and take to a life in the fields while the year he had given his word for was running its course; with other events truly delectable and happy

If a multitude of reflections used to harass Don Quixote before his overthrow, a great many more harassed him since his fall. He was under the shade of a tree, as has been said, and there, like flies on honey, thoughts came crowding upon him and stinging him. Some of them turned on the disenchantment of Dulcinea, others on the life he was about to lead in his enforced retirement. Sancho came up and spoke in high praise of the generous disposition of the lackey Tosilos.

"Is it possible, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that you still think the fellow yonder is a real lackey? Apparently it has slipped your memory that you saw Dulcinea turned and transformed into a peasant wench, and the Knight of the Mirrors into the bachelor Carrasco — all the work of the enchanters that persecute me. But tell me now: did you ask this Tosilos, as you call him, what has become of Altisidora? Did she weep over my absence, or has she already consigned to oblivion the love thoughts that used to torment her when I was there?"

"The thoughts I had," said Sancho, "were not the kind to leave time for asking fool's questions. Body o' me, señor! Is your worship in a condition now to inquire into other people's thoughts, especially love thoughts?"

"Look here, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "there is a great difference between what is done out of love and what is done out of gratitude. A knight may very possibly be proof against love; but it is impossible, strictly speaking, for him to be ungrateful. Altisidora, to all appearances, loved me truly. She gave me the three kerchiefs you know of; she wept at my departure, she cursed me, she abused me, casting shame to the winds she bewailed herself in public — all signs that she adored me; for the wrath of lovers always ends in curses. I had no hopes to give her, no treasures to offer her, for mine are given to Dulcinea, and the treasures of knights-errant are like those of the fairies, illusory and deceptive; all I can give her is the place in my memory I keep for her, without prejudice, however, to the one I hold devoted to Dulcinea — whom you are wronging by your slowness in whipping yourself and scourging that flesh (which I wish I saw eaten by wolves) that would rather keep itself for the worms than for the relief of that poor lady."

"Señor," replied Sancho, "if the truth is to be told, I cannot persuade myself that the whipping of my backside has anything to do with the disenchantment of the enchanted. It's like saying, 'If your head aches, rub ointment on your knees.' At any rate I'll make bold to swear that in all the histories of knight-errantry your worship has read, you've never come across anybody disenchanted by whipping. But, all the same, I'll whip myself when I have a fancy for it, and the opportunity serves for scourging myself comfortably."
"God grant it," said Don Quixote, "and heaven give you grace to take it to heart and acknowledge the obligation you are under to help my lady — who is also yours, inasmuch as you are mine."

As they continued their journey, talking in this way, they came to the very same spot where they had been trampled on by the bulls. Don Quixote recognised it, and said to Sancho, "This is the meadow where we came upon those gay shepherdesses and gallant shepherds who were trying to revive and imitate the pastoral Arcadia there — an idea as novel as it was charming. In imitation of which, if you agree, Sancho, I would have us turn shepherds ourselves, at any rate for the time I have to live in retirement. I'll buy some ewes and everything else the pastoral calling requires; and, with me under the name of the shepherd Quixotize and you as the shepherd Panzino, we'll roam the woods and groves and meadows, singing songs here, lamenting in elegies there, drinking of the crystal waters of the springs, the limpid brooks, the flowing rivers. The oaks will yield us their sweet fruit with a bountiful hand, the trunks of the hard cork trees a seat, the willows shade, the roses perfume, the wide meadows carpets tinted with a thousand dyes; the clear pure air will give us breath, the moon and stars will lighten the darkness of the night for us, song shall be our delight, lamenting our joy, Apollo will supply us with verses, and love with conceits whereby we shall make ourselves famed for ever, not only in this age but in ages to come."

"Egad," said Sancho, "that sort of life squares — nay, corners — with my notions; and what's more, the bachelor Samson Carrasco and Master Nicholas the barber won't have well seen it before they'll want to take it up and turn shepherds along with us; and God grant it doesn't come into the curate's head to join the sheepfold too, he's so jovial and fond of enjoying himself."

"You are quite right, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "and the bachelor Samson Carrasco, if he enters the pastoral fraternity, as he no doubt will, may call himself the shepherd Samsonino, or perhaps the shepherd Carrascon; Nicholas the barber can call himself Niculoso, as old Boscan was once called Nemoroso. As for the curate, I don't know what name we can fit to him unless it be something derived from his title, and we call him the shepherd Curiambro. As for the shepherdesses whose lovers we shall be, we can pick names for them as we would pears; and since my lady's name does just as well for a shepherdess as for a princess, I needn't trouble myself to look for one that will suit her better; you, Sancho, can give yours whatever name you like."

"I don't mean to give her any but Teresona," said Sancho, "which goes well with her stoutness and with her own right name, since she's called Teresa; and when I sing her praises in my verses I'll show how chaste my passion is, for I'm not going to look 'for better bread than ever came from wheat' in other men's houses. It won't do for the curate to have a shepherdess, for the sake of good example; and if the bachelor chooses to have one, that's his lookout."

"God bless me, Sancho my friend!" said Don Quixote, "what a life we shall lead! What hautboys and Zamora bagpipes we'll hear, what tabors, timbrels, and rebecks! And if among all these different sorts of music that of the albogues is heard, almost all the pastoral instruments will be there."
"What are albogues?" asked Sancho, "for I never in my life heard tell of them or saw them."

"Albogues," said Don Quixote, "are brass plates like candlesticks that, struck against one another on the hollow side, make a noise which, if not very pleasing or harmonious, is not disagreeable, and accords very well with the rude notes of the bagpipe and tabor. The word albogue is Morisco, as are all those in our Spanish tongue that begin with _al_ — for example, _almohaza, almorzar, alhombra, alguacil, alhucema, almacen, alcancia_, and others of the same sort, of which there are not many more. Our language has only three that are Morisco and end in _i_, which are _borceguí, zaquizamí_, and _maravedí. Alhelí_ and _alfaquí_ are seen to be Arabic, as well by the _al_ at the beginning as by the _í_ they end with. I mention this in passing, the chance allusion to albogues having reminded me of it; and it will be a great help to us in the perfect practice of this calling that I am something of a poet, as you know, and that besides, the bachelor Samson Carrasco is an accomplished one. Of the curate I say nothing; but I'll wager he has some spice of the poet in him, and no doubt Master Nicholas too, for all barbers, or most of them, are guitar players and stringers of verses. I will lament my separation; you will glorify yourself as a constant lover; the shepherd Carrascon will figure as a rejected one, and the curate Curiambro as whatever may please him best; and so all will go as merrily as heart could wish."

To this Sancho answered, "I'm so unlucky, señor, that I'm afraid the day will never come when I'll see myself at such a calling. Oh, what neat spoons I'll make when I'm a shepherd! What messes, creams, garlands, pastoral odds and ends! And if they don't get me a name for wisdom, they won't fail to get me one for ingenuity. My daughter Sanchica will bring us our dinner to the pasture. But hold on — she's good-looking, and there are shepherds about with more mischief than simplicity in them; I wouldn't have her 'come for wool and go back shorn.' Love-making and lawless desires are just as common in the fields as in cities, and in shepherds' shanties as in royal palaces; 'do away with the cause, you do away with the sin;' 'if eyes don't see, hearts don't break,' and 'better a clear escape than good men's prayers.'"

"A truce to your proverbs, Sancho," exclaimed Don Quixote; "any one of those you have uttered would suffice to explain your meaning; many a time I have recommended you not to be so lavish with proverbs and to exercise some moderation in delivering them; but it seems to me it's only 'preaching in the desert;' 'my mother beats me and I go on with my tricks.'"

"It seems to me," said Sancho, "that your worship is like the common saying, 'Said the frying-pan to the kettle, get away, blackbreech.' You chide me for uttering proverbs, and you string them in couples yourself."

"Observe, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "I bring in proverbs to the purpose, and when I quote them they fit like a ring to the finger; you bring them in by the head and shoulders, in such a way that you drag them in, rather than introduce them. If I am not mistaken, I have told you already that proverbs are short maxims drawn from the experience and observation of our wise men of old; but the proverb that is not to the purpose is a piece of nonsense and not a maxim. But enough of this; as nightfall is drawing on, let us retire some little distance from the high road to pass the night; what is in store for us tomorrow God knows."

They turned aside, and supped late and poorly, very much against Sancho's will, who turned over in his mind the hardships attendant on knight-errantry in woods and forests, even though at times plenty showed itself in castles and houses, as at Don Diego de Miranda's, at the wedding of Camacho the Rich, and at Don Antonio Moreno's; he reflected, however, that it could not always be day, nor always night; and so that night he spent in sleeping, and his master in waking.

title: Part 2, Chapter 68
paragraphs: About the bristly adventure that befell Don Quixote

The night was somewhat dark, for though there was a moon in the sky, she was not in a quarter where she could be seen; for sometimes the lady Diana goes on a stroll to the antipodes, and leaves the mountains all black and the valleys in darkness. Don Quixote obeyed nature so far as to sleep his first sleep, but did not give way to the second — very different from Sancho, who never had any second, because with him sleep lasted from night till morning, by which he showed what a sound constitution he had and how few cares. Don Quixote's cares kept him restless, so much so that he woke Sancho and said to him, "I am amazed, Sancho, at the unconcern of your temperament. I believe you are made of marble or hard brass, incapable of any emotion or feeling whatever. I lie awake while you sleep, I weep while you sing, I am faint with fasting while you are sluggish and torpid from pure repletion. It is the duty of good servants to share the sufferings and feel the sorrows of their masters, if only for appearances' sake. See the calmness of the night, the solitude of the spot, inviting us to break our slumbers by a vigil of some sort. Get up, as you live, and step a little distance away, and with a good heart and cheerful courage give yourself three or four hundred lashes on account of Dulcinea's disenchantment; and this I beg of you, making it a request, for I have no desire to come to grips with you a second time, as I know you have a heavy hand. Once you've laid them on, we'll pass the rest of the night, I singing my separation, you your constancy, making a start at once with the pastoral life we are to follow at our village."

"Señor," replied Sancho, "I'm no monk to get up out of the middle of my sleep and scourge myself, nor does it seem to me that one can pass from one extreme of the pain of whipping to the other of music. Will your worship let me sleep, and not bother me about whipping myself? Or you'll make me swear never to touch a hair of my doublet, let alone my flesh."

"Oh hard heart!" said Don Quixote, "Oh pitiless squire! Oh bread ill-bestowed and favours ill-acknowledged, both those I have done you and those I mean to do you! Through me you have seen yourself a governor, and through me you see yourself on the verge of being a count, or obtaining some other equivalent title, for I — _post tenebras spero lucem_."

"I don't know what that is," said Sancho; "all I know is that as long as I'm asleep I have neither fear nor hope, trouble nor glory; and good luck to whoever invented sleep — the cloak that covers over all a man's thoughts, the food that removes hunger, the drink that drives away thirst, the fire that warms the cold, the cold that tempers the heat, and, to wind up with, the universal coin with which everything is bought, the weight and balance that makes the shepherd equal with the king and the fool with the wise man. Sleep, I have heard say, has only one fault — that it's like death; for between a sleeping man and a dead one there's very little difference."

"Never have I heard you speak so elegantly as now, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "and here I begin to see the truth of the proverb you sometimes quote, 'Not with whom you are bred, but with whom you are fed.'"

"Ha, by my life, master mine," said Sancho, "it's not I that am stringing proverbs now, for they drop in pairs from your worship's mouth faster than from mine; only there's this difference between mine and yours, that yours are well-timed and mine are untimely; but either way, they're all proverbs."

At this point they became aware of a harsh indistinct noise that seemed to spread through all the valleys around. Don Quixote stood up and laid his hand upon his sword, and Sancho ensconced himself under Dapple and put the bundle of armour on one side of him and the ass's pack-saddle on the other, in fear and trembling as great as Don Quixote's perturbation. Each instant the noise grew louder and came nearer to the two terrified men — or at least to one, for as to the other, his courage is known to all. The truth of the matter was that some men were taking above six hundred pigs to sell at a fair, and were on their way with them at that hour, and so great was the noise they made, with their grunting and snorting, that they deafened the ears of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, who could not make out what it was. The wide-spread grunting drove came on in a surging mass, and without showing any respect for Don Quixote's dignity or Sancho's, passed right over the pair of them, demolishing Sancho's entrenchments, and not only knocking Don Quixote down but sweeping Rocinante off his feet into the bargain; and what with the trampling, the grunting, and the pace at which the unclean beasts went, pack-saddle, armour, Dapple, and Rocinante were left scattered on the ground and Sancho and Don Quixote at their wits' end.

Sancho got up as best he could and begged his master to give him his sword, saying he wanted to kill half a dozen of those dirty unmannerly pigs, since he had by this time figured out that that was what they were.

"Let them be, my friend," said Don Quixote; "this insult is the penalty of my sin; and it is the righteous chastisement of heaven that jackals should devour a vanquished knight, that wasps should sting him and pigs trample him underfoot."

"I suppose it's the chastisement of heaven too," said Sancho, "that flies should prick the squires of vanquished knights, and lice eat them, and hunger assail them. If we squires were the sons of the knights we serve, or their very near relations, it would be no wonder if the penalty of their misdeeds overtook us, even to the fourth generation. But what have the Panzas got to do with the Quixotes? Well, well, let's lie down again and sleep out what little of the night is left, and God will send us dawn and we'll be all right."

"Sleep, Sancho," returned Don Quixote, "for you were born to sleep as I was born to watch; and during what's left before dawn I'll give a loose rein to my thoughts, and find a vent for them in a little madrigal which, unknown to you, I composed in my head last night."

"I should think," said Sancho, "that thoughts that allow one to make verses can't be of any great consequence; let your worship string verses as much as you like, and I'll sleep as much as I can." And forthwith, taking the space of ground he required, he muffled himself up and fell into a sound sleep, undisturbed by bond, debt, or trouble of any sort. Don Quixote, propped up against the trunk of a beech or a cork tree — for Cide Hamete does not specify what kind of tree it was — sang in this strain to the accompaniment of his own sighs:
_When in my mind I muse, O Love, upon thy cruelty, / To death I flee, / In hope therein the end of all to find._
_But drawing near / That welcome haven in my sea of woe, / Such joy I know, / That life revives, and still I linger here._
_Thus life doth slay, / And death again to life restoreth me; / Strange destiny, / That deals with life and death as with a play!_
He accompanied each verse with many sighs and not a few tears, just like one whose heart was pierced with grief at his defeat and his separation from Dulcinea.

And now daylight came, and the sun smote Sancho on the eyes with his beams. He woke, roused himself, shook himself, and stretched his lazy limbs, and seeing the havoc the pigs had made of his stores, he cursed the drove, and more besides. Then the pair resumed their journey, and as evening closed in they saw coming towards them some ten men on horseback and four or five on foot. Don Quixote's heart beat quick and Sancho's quailed with fear, for the men approaching them carried lances and shields, and were got up in very warlike fashion. Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said, "If I could use my weapons, and my promise had not tied my hands, I'd count this host coming against us as cakes and fancy bread; but perhaps it may turn out to be something other than what we fear." The men on horseback now came up, and raising their lances surrounded Don Quixote in silence, and pointed them at his back and breast, threatening him with death. One of those on foot, putting his finger to his lips as a signal for silence, seized Rocinante's bridle and drew him out of the road, and the others drove Sancho and Dapple before them, all maintaining a strange silence, and followed in the steps of the one who led Don Quixote. Don Quixote two or three times tried to ask where they were taking him and what they wanted, but the instant he began to open his lips they threatened to close them with the points of their lances; and Sancho fared the same way, for the moment he seemed about to speak one of those on foot punched him with a goad, and Dapple likewise, as if he too wanted to talk. Night set in, they quickened their pace, and the fears of the two prisoners grew greater, especially as they heard themselves assailed with — "Get on, you Troglodytes;" "Silence, you barbarians;" "March, you cannibals;" "No murmuring, you Scythians;" "Don't open your eyes, you murderous Polyphemes, you bloodthirsty lions," and other names of the kind with which their captors harassed the ears of the wretched master and man. Sancho went along saying to himself, "We, tortolites, barbers, animals! I don't like those names at all; 'it's in a bad wind our corn is being winnowed;' 'misfortune comes upon us all at once like sticks on a dog,' and God grant it may be no worse than them that this unlucky adventure has in store for us."

Don Quixote rode along completely dazed, unable, even with all his wits, to make out the meaning of these abusive names they called them, and the only conclusion he could come to was that there was no good to be hoped for and much evil to be feared. And now, about an hour after midnight, they reached a castle which Don Quixote at once recognised as the duke's, where they had been not long before. "God bless me!" he said, as he recognised the mansion, "what does this mean? It is all courtesy and politeness in this house — but with the vanquished, good turns into evil, and evil into worse."
They entered the chief court of the castle, and found it prepared and fitted up in a style that added to their amazement and doubled their fears — as will be seen in the following chapter.

title: Part 2, Chapter 69
paragraphs: Concerning the strangest and most extraordinary adventure that happened to Don Quixote in the entire course of this great history

The horsemen dismounted, and together with the men on foot they lifted Sancho and Don Quixote bodily, without a moment's pause, and carried them into the courtyard. Around its whole perimeter nearly a hundred torches burned in their sockets, with more than five hundred lamps along the corridors besides, so that although the night was fairly dark, no one could have missed the daylight. In the middle of the courtyard stood a catafalque, raised about two yards off the ground and draped entirely in an enormous canopy of black velvet, and on the steps surrounding it white wax tapers burned in more than a hundred silver candlesticks. On the catafalque lay the dead body of a young woman so lovely that her beauty made death itself look beautiful. Her head rested on a brocade cushion and was crowned with a garland of fragrant flowers of many kinds; her hands were crossed on her breast, and between them lay a branch of yellow victory palm. On one side of the courtyard a stage had been erected, where two figures sat on two chairs; the crowns on their heads and the scepters in their hands suggested they were kings of some description, whether genuine or theatrical. Beside this stage, which was reached by a flight of steps, stood two more chairs, and on these the men carrying the prisoners seated Don Quixote and Sancho, all in complete silence, indicating by gestures that they too were to keep quiet—though they would have done so without any prompting, since astonishment at everything they were seeing had left them speechless. Now two persons of obvious rank, whom Don Quixote immediately recognized as his hosts the duke and duchess, climbed onto the stage with a large retinue and took their places on two magnificent chairs beside the two apparent kings. Who would not have been astounded by all this? And that was not the whole of it, for Don Quixote had realized that the dead body on the catafalque was that of the beautiful Altisidora. As the duke and duchess mounted the stage, Don Quixote and Sancho rose and bowed deeply to them, and they answered with a slight inclination of their heads. At that moment an official crossed the courtyard, came up to Sancho, and threw over him a robe of black buckram painted all over with flames of fire; then, removing his cap, he set on his head a mitre of the kind worn by those sentenced by the Holy Office, whispering in his ear that he must not open his mouth or they would gag him, or kill him. Sancho looked himself over from head to foot and saw that he was blazing with flames; but since they did not burn him, he did not care two farthings about them. He took off the mitre, saw that it was painted with devils, and put it back on, saying to himself, "Well, so far the flames aren't burning me and the devils aren't carrying me off." Don Quixote looked him over as well, and although fear had overwhelmed his senses, he could not help smiling at the figure Sancho cut. And now, from beneath the catafalque it seemed, there rose a low, sweet sound of flutes which, unbroken by any human voice—for there silence itself kept silence—had a soft and melting effect. Then, suddenly, beside the pillow of what appeared to be the corpse, a handsome youth dressed in the Roman style appeared, and to the accompaniment of a harp that he played himself, he sang these two stanzas in a sweet, clear voice:

While fair Altisidora, made the toy
of cold Don Quixote's unfeeling cruelty,
returns to life, and in this enchanted court
the ladies dress in sables for the scene,
and while her matrons, all in proper form,
robe my lady in baize and bombazine,
I will sing her beauty and her sorrows here
with a defter quill than ever struck the Thracian string.

But it is not in life alone, I think,
that this office falls to me; Lady, when my tongue
lies cold in death, believe me, even then
my voice will raise its tribute song to you.
My soul, set free from this cramped prison-house,
drifting along across the Stygian lake,
will go its way still singing in your praise,
and make the waters of oblivion stand still.

At this point one of the two who looked like kings called out, "Enough, enough, divine singer! It would take forever to recount for us now the death and the charms of the peerless Altisidora—who is not dead, as the ignorant world supposes, but alive in the voice of fame and in the penance that Sancho Panza, here present, must undergo to restore her to the light she has lost. Therefore, O Rhadamanthus, you who sit in judgment with me in the murky caverns of Dis, since you know everything the inscrutable fates have decreed concerning the revival of this damsel, announce and declare it at once, so that the happiness we expect from her restoration is delayed no longer."
Scarcely had Minos, Rhadamanthus's fellow judge, finished saying this when Rhadamanthus stood up and declared:

"Ho, officials of this house, high and low, great and small, hurry here every one of you, and plant twenty-four smacks on Sancho's face, and give him twelve pinches and six pin-pricks in the back and arms; for on this ceremony depends the restoration of Altisidora."

When Sancho heard this he broke his silence and cried out, "By all that's holy, I'll let my face be smacked and pawed at the day I turn Moor. Body of me! What does manhandling my face have to do with this damsel's resurrection? 'The old woman took kindly to the blits.' They enchant Dulcinea, and I get whipped to disenchant her; Altisidora dies of whatever ailments God chose to send her, and to bring her back to life I have to take twenty-four smacks, have my body punctured with pins, and have my arms pinched until they're covered in welts! Try those jokes on a brother-in-law; 'I'm an old dog, and tus, tus doesn't work on me.'"

"You shall die," said Rhadamanthus in a loud voice. "Relent, you tiger; humble yourself, proud Nimrod; suffer and be silent, for nothing impossible is being asked of you, and it is not your place to question the difficulties of this matter. Smacked you must be, pricked you shall find yourself, and pinched until you howl. Come, officials, I say, carry out my orders—or, on the word of an honest man, you will see what you were born for."

At this, some six duennas appeared, advancing across the courtyard in procession one behind the other, four of them wearing spectacles, and all with their right hands raised, showing four fingers' width of wrist to make their hands look longer, as the fashion now dictates. The moment Sancho caught sight of them he bellowed like a bull and shouted, "I might let the whole world handle me, but let duennas touch me—never! Scratch my face, the way my master was treated in this very castle; run me through the body with polished daggers; pinch my arms with red-hot pincers—I'll bear it all patiently to oblige these noble people. But I won't let duennas lay a finger on me, even if the devil carries me off!"

Here Don Quixote broke his silence too, saying to Sancho, "Be patient, my son, and oblige these noble persons, and give heaven all your thanks for having placed such virtue in your person that through its sufferings you can disenchant the enchanted and bring the dead back to life."

By now the duennas were close upon Sancho, and he, grown more docile and reasonable, settled himself properly in his chair and offered his face and beard to the first of them, who delivered a very firmly planted smack and then dropped him a low curtsey.
"Less courtesy and less face-paint, señora duenna," said Sancho; "by God, your hands smell of vinegar-wash."

One after another, all the duennas smacked him, and several other members of the household pinched him; but what he could not endure was the pricking of the pins. So, his patience apparently exhausted, he sprang up from his chair, seized a lighted torch standing nearby, and went after the duennas and the whole crew of his tormentors, shouting, "Away with you, ministers of hell! I'm not made of brass, that I should feel nothing under such outlandish tortures."

At that instant Altisidora—who was probably tired of lying on her back for so long—turned onto her side, and at the sight of it the onlookers cried out almost in one voice, "Altisidora is alive! Altisidora lives!"

Rhadamanthus ordered Sancho to lay aside his anger, since the purpose they had been pursuing was now achieved. The moment Don Quixote saw Altisidora stir, he dropped to his knees before Sancho and said to him, "Now is the moment, son of my heart—not merely my squire—for you to give yourself some of those lashes you are bound to administer for the disenchantment of Dulcinea. Now, I say, is the time when the virtue within you is ripe and charged with power to work the good that is expected of you."

To which Sancho replied, "That's trick piled on trick, if you ask me, and not honey on pancakes. A fine thing it would be to get a whipping now, on top of pinches, smacks, and pin-jabbings! You might as well tie a big stone around my neck and throw me down a well—I'd hardly mind, if I'm forever to be made the wedding-cow that pays for curing other people's ailments. Leave me alone, or by God I'll throw the whole business to the dogs, come what may."

By this time Altisidora had sat up on the catafalque, and as she did, the clarions rang out, joined by the flutes and by the voices of everyone present crying, "Long live Altisidora! Long live Altisidora!" The duke and duchess and the kings Minos and Rhadamanthus rose to their feet, and all of them, together with Don Quixote and Sancho, went forward to receive her and help her down from the catafalque. She, acting as though she were just coming out of a faint, bowed her head to the duke and duchess and to the kings, and glancing sideways at Don Quixote, said to him, "God forgive you, unfeeling knight, for thanks to your cruelty I have spent what feels to me like more than a thousand years in the other world; and to you, the most compassionate man on earth, I give thanks for the life I now enjoy. From this day forward, friend Sancho, count as yours six smocks of mine, which I give you to make into as many shirts for yourself; and if they are not all entirely whole, at least they are all clean."

Sancho kissed her hands in gratitude, kneeling, with the mitre in his hand. The duke ordered it taken from him, his cap and doublet returned, and the flaming robe removed. Sancho begged the duke to let him keep the robe and mitre, since he wanted to carry them home as a token and keepsake of that unparalleled adventure. The duchess said they must indeed be left with him, for he already knew what a great friend of his she was. The duke then gave orders for the courtyard to be cleared, for everyone to withdraw to their rooms, and for Don Quixote and Sancho to be escorted back to their old quarters.
